The simulations evaluate total evacuation time, occupant flow and congestion under different design scenarios while also assessing compliance with selected Saudi Building Code (SBC) egress requirements. Findings The simulations show that total evacuation time remains relatively high across all scenarios. However, stair placement and wider egress doors improve efficiency, while adding extra stairs in some layouts offers only limited benefit. Research limitations/implications The study highlights the challenges of achieving substantial improvements through design modifications. It identifies directions for future research on how design decisions influence emergency evacuation efficiency. Practical implications The research provides fire safety engineers, architects and emergency planners with insights into how selected design decisions influence evacuation efficiency in high-rise residential buildings. The findings support interventions such as optimizing stair location, assessing stair width and widening egress doors to reduce congestion and improve evacuation performance. Originality/value This study presents a BIM-based case of evacuation performance in a high-rise residential building in Saudi Arabia and assesses its compliance with selected SBC egress requirements. It provides context-specific evidence on how design variables affect evacuation efficiency.
k: building evacuation; high-rise residential buildings; fire emergencies; evacuation time; evacuation congestion; Pathfinder simulation

journal: Millennial Asia: An International Journal of Asian Studies
t: Can Human Capital Mitigate the Environmental Costs of Urbanization? Empirical Evidence from Asia’s Five Largest Economies
a: Rapid urbanization in Asia has intensified concerns over rising CO 2 emissions, yet the moderating influence of human capital in this process remains underexplored. This study examines whether human capital can mitigate the environmental impact of urbanization in five major Asian economies—China, India, Japan, South Korea and Indonesia—during 1990–2021. Employing advanced panel econometric techniques, including cross-sectional dependence tests, panel co-integration analysis and a panel ARDL framework with Panel Mean Group (PMG), MG and DFE estimators, the study captures both long- and short-run dynamics. Robustness is ensured through dynamic OLS estimation, while Granger causality and variance decomposition provide insights into the direction and strength of causal linkages. The results reveal that urbanization significantly increases CO 2 emissions, with a 1% rise in the urban population contributing to a 7.53% increase in emissions. In contrast, human capital directly reduces emissions by 1.68% and, when interacting with urbanization, offsets its adverse effect by 11.76%. Evidence broadly supports the Environmental Kuznets Curve, although country-specific heterogeneity emerges: human capital fosters sustainable urbanization in China and South Korea, and moderates environmental stress in India, while financial development intensifies emissions in Japan and Indonesia. By quantifying the moderating role of human capital, this study adds novel evidence to the environmental economics literature and underscores human capital development as a key policy instrument for achieving sustainable urban growth and low-carbon development in Asia.
k: human capital; urbanization; CO2 emissions; environmental Kuznets curve; moderating effect; sustainable urbanization; financial development; low-carbon development; Asian economies; China; India; Japan; South Korea; Indonesia

journal: Journal of Electronic Commerce in Organizations
t: Key Focus Areas in the Literature on Organic SEO Strategies for E-Commerce: A Systematic Literature Review
a: The article develops a systematic literature review examining the fundamental role of organic Search Engine Optimization (SEO) in electronic commerce (e-commerce). The PRISMA method guided the review process. Through the analysis of a large corpus using textometric and semantic techniques, the study identifies and analyzes the most frequently used terms and concepts in academic research on organic SEO in e-commerce. The findings confirm that SEO strategies significantly influence visibility, traffic, and overall platform performance. The review also categorizes recent trends and innovative approaches, including keyword optimization, high-quality content creation, and integration with broader digital marketing strategies. The study highlights substantial opportunities for future research and outlines relevant managerial implications. As e-commerce continues to expand, adaptive and innovative SEO strategies are essential to ensure sustained competitiveness in an increasingly dynamic digital environment.
k: e-commerce; keyword optimization; content marketing; digital marketing strategy; website traffic; online visibility; search engine ranking

journal: SERIEs: Journal of the Spanish Economic Association
t: Women and willingness to guess: an investigation using a high-stake test in the Spanish health sector
a: Multiple-choice tests are the gateway to important professional outcomes in the Spanish health sector. Every year, thousands of nursing, psychology, pharmacy, and biology graduates take a multiple-choice test, with wrong answers penalized, in order to access an intern position in a hospital. In such tests, willingness to guess , the decision to provide an answer instead of omitting the question can have a differential effect on the overall performance. This paper first studies the evolution of gender differences in willingness to guess, measured by the proportion of answered questions, over a 40-year period. Second, we exploit a natural experiment that occurred between 2014 and 2015, when the number of alternative answers was reduced from 5 to 4, effectively lowering the penalty for incorrect answers, to test for gender differential reactions in willingness to guess.
k: gender differences; multiple-choice tests; nursing graduates; medical internship; test-taking behavior

t: What do we know about sustainability reporting assurance quality?
a: The assurance of sustainability and CSR reporting has emerged as an important mechanism for enhancing the credibility and reliability of non-financial disclosures. Although assurance practices have expanded rapidly, academic evidence regarding their quality, determinants, and consequences remains fragmented and is still evolving. This paper synthesizes the historical development of CSR assurance, outlines its core objectives, evaluates existing evidence on assurance quality, and identifies key gaps and avenues for future research. In doing so, we offer a critical assessment of what is known and what remains unknown about CSR assurance as it gains prominence in corporate accountability and the functioning of capital markets.
k: sustainability reporting; quality assurance; corporate social responsibility disclosure; non-financial reporting; corporate accountability; capital markets

t: The Role of the Invasion of Afghanistan and Reputation in President Carter's Handling of the Iran Hostage Crisis: Prioritizing International Over Domestic Factors
a: President Carter's handling of the Iran Hostage Crisis was an archetypal example of the influence of presidential personality and domestic factors on force preference decision-making. Carter's worldview allegedly led him to prioritize hostage safety and shun the use of force. However, this article presents a revisionist account of the crisis based on newly declassified documents that demonstrates that international factors, including the invasion of Afghanistan, the regional balance of power, and American credibility were determinative. Contrary to his reputation as a weak leader, Carter actively sought a military solution to the conflict, but his ability to act was constrained by the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. Following the invasion, Carter's focus shifted from using force against Iran to deterring a Soviet invasion of the country. The article alters the current understanding of the crisis and challenges the dominance of personality and domestic factors in the use of force decision-making literature.
k: Iranian hostage crisis; Carter administration; presidential reputation; Soviet invasion of Afghanistan; regional balance of power; hostage rescue; military intervention; presidential personality; domestic politics and foreign policy

t: Does family ownership benefit non-listed firms? Evidence from family-owned non-listed insurance companies in Thailand
a: This study investigates the performance of family and non-family firms while isolating the impact of stock market listing in Thailand's non-life insurance industry, where listed and non-listed insurers are comparable in size and age. Results show that family ownership negatively relates to performance among non-listed firms and that non-listed family firms underperform both non-family and listed family firms. Evidence also suggests that non-listed family-owned insurers engage in excessive risk-taking consistent with wealth expropriation. Our findings question the superior performance of family firms often documented in the literature because benefits of stock market listing could potentially be the confounding factors.
k: family ownership; non-listed companies; stock market listing; firm performance; family business; excessive risk-taking; wealth expropriation; Thailand

t: The post-study abroad experience in Japan: student reintegration as future global human resources
a: The cultivation of global jinzai, or ‘global human resources’ (GHR), has become a key goal of Japanese higher education, and student mobility programs have been widely promoted as a way to foster the skills deemed desirable in Japanese GHR. Research suggests that study abroad may impact the career trajectory of students in Japan, but little is known about the experiences of student returnees and how their skills as GHR are cultivated, appraised, and utilized in a domestic setting post-study abroad. This article presents the results of a qualitative study designed to investigate the post-study abroad experiences of university students in Japan. Seven mini-focus groups were conducted at national, public, and private universities with students (N = 14) who had spent at least one semester abroad. Thematic content analysis revealed reintegration challenges in relation to students’ job-hunting activities and career paths. Findings suggest a disconnect between the industry push for GHR and hiring practices experienced by students. This article explores the challenges affecting the successful re-entry of students into Japan as well as the impact of study abroad on students’ search for employment. Finally, it suggests ways in which universities and potential employers can continue to foster and utilize student GHR competencies post-study abroad.
k: study abroad; student reintegration; global human resources; student mobility; returnees; job search; career paths; hiring practices; internationalization of higher education; Japanese universities; employability

journal: International Journal of Intellectual Property Management
t: Exploring Ethiopia's intellectual property rights system: prospects and grey areas for agro-food chain sector innovations
a: Ethiopia, one of the most agriculturally viable and biodiverse countries in Sub-Saharan Africa, continues to face food insecurity. Strengthening the intellectual property rights (IPR) regime could play a critical role in fostering innovation and supporting the country's transition toward sustainable food security. This explorative study assessed Ethiopia's IPR frameworks through article-by-article analysis, synthesising local and international legal documents to provide a comprehensive narrative analysis of their potential to drive agricultural innovation. The findings indicate that Ethiopia's IPR system, covering copyright, patents, plant breeders' rights, and trademarks, contains provisions that may encourage agricultural innovation. While Ethiopia's alignment with international IPR treaties reflects its readiness to embrace innovation, gaps remain, including conflicts with certain accords, a lack of protection of geographical indications and traditional knowledge, weak institutional capacity, and limited enforcement. The study underscores the need to implement a geographical indications system and a sui generis framework for traditional knowledge. It also calls for revisions to the Plant Breeders' Rights Proclamation to ensure administrative coordination, alongside stronger institutions and empirical research on monopolistic practices, biodiversity loss, and biopiracy to enhance IPR's role in agricultural innovation and food security.
k: intellectual property; Ethiopia; agricultural innovation; agri-food supply chains; food security; plant breeders' rights; geographical indications; traditional knowledge; sui generis protection; copyright; patents; trademarks; IPR enforcement; biopiracy; biodiversity loss

t: What is Strasbourg’s theory of environmental human rights?
a: Although the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) contains no explicit environmental right, the Strasbourg Court has gradually come to afford the environment considerable protection under Articles 2 and 8 of the ECHR. Until recently, commentators generally saw this protection as nothing more than a patchwork of discrete decisions. By the early 2020s, however, scholars had recognized that the protection went beyond a patchwork and constituted a coherent set of environmental obligations. The prevailing view, nevertheless, remains that the Court does not recognize a standalone environmental human right. This article challenges that view. It argues that the Court’s environmental jurisprudence amounts to something approaching a standalone, if narrowly drawn, right to a safe and healthy environment, which is especially apparent in its recent jurisprudence. The wider implication is that while the Court may in general be ‘walking back rights’, it appears to be marching forward in the environmental domain.
k: environmental human rights; European Convention on Human Rights; European Court of Human Rights; Article 2 ECHR; right to respect for private and family life; environmental obligations; environmental case law

t: Assessing the Role of Board, Culture and Environmental Complexity on Performance Information Use in Nonprofit Organizations
a: Despite growing expectations for Nonprofit Organizations to implement performance measurement, empirical research on its actual use remains limited. To address such a gap, this study investigates the decision-facilitating use of performance information focusing on environmental complexities, the role of the board of directors, and organizational culture. The empirical setting is provided by Nonprofit Organizations located in the province of Bergamo (Italy) to which a survey was administered. The analysis shows that environmental complexity does not directly increase the use of performance information. Rather, it operates indirectly through an externally oriented board and a flexible culture, both serving as bridges that connect external pressures to internal systems.
k: performance information use; nonprofit organizations; board of directors; organizational culture; environmental complexity; performance measurement; decision-making; Bergamo

t: Extreme Capital Flows and Risk Linkages in Emerging Market Financial Submarkets
a: This paper examines the drivers and impacts of extreme capital flow events in emerging markets, with a focus on distinguishing among flow types (portfolio, bank and FDI) and event categories (surge vs. stop). We find that the global financial cycle drives extreme events in portfolio and bank flows, while FDI is more sensitive to domestic factors. Notably, sudden stops in cross‐border capital flows, particularly in bank and FDI flows, have a greater impact on the overall risk interconnectedness of domestic financial submarkets compared to surge events. We also identify the transmission channels: extreme bank flow events increase credit market net risk spillovers, while concurrent extreme capital flow events heighten foreign exchange market net risk spillovers. Further discussion shows that foreign exchange sales and macroprudential policies mitigate the adverse effects of negative global financial cycle shocks, with macroprudential measures demonstrating stronger effectiveness in the medium term.
k: sudden stops; capital flow surges; emerging markets; global financial cycle; portfolio investment; bank lending; foreign direct investment; macroprudential policy

t: Open source digital sovereignty: the case for a Canadian national Linux distribution
a: Purpose The post-2020 global pivot toward digital sovereignty has been accelerated for Canada by a rupture in trust with the USA: 60% of Canadians report they can no longer trust the USA, while the Clarifying Lawful Overseas Use of Data Act and Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act §702 grant extraterritorial access to data held by the US-headquartered providers regardless of physical location. Despite this exposure, Canada’s federal government remains structurally dependent on a single US vendor for its foundational software stack: Microsoft Windows controls 58% of Canada’s desktop market, federal Microsoft contracts exceeded C$865m over 10 years and Windows-specific licensing alone is C$108m–C$126m/year. Operating systems remain absent from Canadian sovereignty debates dominated by cloud, AI and 5G. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the strategic autonomy and economic impact of a Canadian national Linux distribution. Design/methodology/approach This paper develops a comparative policy analysis of six state-sponsored Linux distributions (China, Russia, India, France, Germany and South Korea) using a dual total cost of ownership (TCO) + strategic autonomy analytical framework, benchmarked against Canada’s procurement landscape, laws and trade obligations. Findings Conservative net 10-year savings of C$350m–C$965m (net present value at 5% discount rate) are achievable, calibrated against GendBuntu’s documented €500m savings, the Italian Ministry of Defense’s €26m–€29m migration and Ghosh’s 36% public-sector TCO reduction. The proposal generates 10-year return on investments of 700%–4,100% on C$23m–C$43m investment and an internal rate of return of 55%–105%. Originality/value This paper proposes a Canadian Free and Open Systems Foundation (Crown not-for-profit modeled on Germany’s Zentrum für Digitale Souveränität) alongside a three-phase implementation roadmap and five institutionally targeted policy recommendations. The proposal offers a generalizable middle-power template for reconciling digital sovereignty with open multilateralism, applicable to Australia, Japan, South Korea and Nordic states facing parallel dependencies.
k: digital sovereignty; open source software; strategic autonomy; total cost of ownership; Canadian federal government; foreign intelligence surveillance

t: Uncertainty-aware multi-objective optimization for rebalancing bike shared systems
a: Overnight rebalancing in dock-based bike-sharing systems requires routing a limited fleet of trucks before user activity begins. This article formulates static rebalancing problem under stochastic demand uncertainty as a bi-objective combinatorial optimization problem that selects truck routes and visited stations. The first objective minimizes total travel distance. The second objective minimizes scenario-weighted unmet demand under a finite set of demand scenarios derived from historical station-status data. A deterministic recourse evaluation simulates truck loads and station inventories along each route and computes unmet demand for visited and unvisited stations. The article applies two multi-objective evolutionary algorithms, NSGA-II and MOEA/D, using a permutation–partition encoding and relocate-based operators that implement a 1–0 relocate neighborhood between routes. A roulette-wheel-based relocation operator (BB2) biases move selection by the induced change in route distance. Experiments on the Barcelona Bicing network with 518 stations and on clustered subinstances show that NSGA-II attains higher hypervolume and larger non-dominated sets, whereas MOEA/D attains lower runtime; an ablation analysis shows that BB2 improves coverage and proximity indicators.
k: bike sharing; truck routing; unmet demand; multi-objective evolutionary algorithms; NSGA-II; MOEA/D

t: Beyond control: a phenomenological inquiry into leader and follower micromanagement experiences
a: Purpose This study examines the experiential meanings of micromanagement within organizations from managers’ and employees’ perspectives to identify its essential structure. Design/methodology/approach Employing a phenomenological analysis, this study investigated the experiences of 18 participants (9 managers, 9 employees) selected based on criteria such as managerial/employee status and prior micromanagement exposure. Findings Managers perceived micromanagement as a complex phenomenon intricately linked to their internal anxiety, role performance pressure, employee perceptions, and relational experiences, beyond mere suppressive behavior. Employees, conversely, experienced continuous monitoring and intervention, leading to a profound loss of autonomy, restricted decision-making, and increased relational distance. However, some positive perceptions were noted, where managers’ behaviors were subjectively interpreted as educational support stemming from recognition and interest. Practical implications The findings suggest the need for human resource development programs addressing managers’ anxiety and role pressure, management styles considering employee career stages, and communication efforts to bridge perceptual gaps. By identifying micromanagement’s essential nature, this study aims to foster a nuanced understanding of its complex reality, moving beyond simplistic views, and contributing to more effective leadership and followership. Originality/value This study reconceptualizes micromanagement, offering an expanded conceptual understanding and proposing new research directions. It also provides a micro-level extension of resource dependence theory for relational phenomena.
k: micromanagement; leader-follower relationships; employee autonomy; relational distance; employee monitoring; management style; human resource development; resource dependence theory; leadership; followership; experiential meaning

t: How close is New Zealand to its revenue-maximising top tax rate?
a: This note asks how close New Zealand’s 39% top personal income tax rate is to the revenue-maximising rate. Using Inland Revenue taxable-income tabulations for FY2010–FY2024, we estimate the concentration of income above the top threshold and apply a sufficient-statistics approach based on the elasticity of taxable income to top-rate revenue analysis. Benchmark calculations place the current top rate below the revenue-maximising point, but the margin is more modest in practice once GST and stronger top-end responses are taken into account. Any practical headroom above 39% depends heavily on taxable-income responses and on whether a higher top rate is accompanied by policies that protect the tax base, including anti-avoidance provisions.
k: revenue maximization; tax rate elasticity; taxable income; income concentration; tax base protection; anti-avoidance provisions; general sales tax; tax revenue

t: The effects of minimum wage regulation in inter‐regional oligopoly competition
a: We examine how minimum wage regulation affects firm profit when labor‐market power interacts with product‐market competition. A binding wage floor reduces the regulated firm's marginal labor cost, inducing it to expand production. This expansion can induce rivals to contract production when relevant strategic variables are strategic substitutes. The mechanism can raise the regulated firm's profit as well as total employment and consumer surplus. We characterize the conditions for profit enhancement and show how labor‐market linkages alter strategic interaction. For instance, in a differentiated‐product Bertrand duopoly with a shared duopsony component, prices can become strategic substitutes, yielding a related profit‐enhancing mechanism.
k: minimum wage legislation; wage floor; oligopolistic competition; interregional competition; labor market power; strategic substitutes; Bertrand duopoly; firm profitability; employment; consumer surplus; differentiated products; strategic interaction

t: Nonviolent protest and ideological change in education: a public choice approach
a: This paper applies a public choice framework to examine how successful nonviolent protest campaigns are associated with changes in the ideological orientation of state education systems. We conceptualize education as a site of political bargaining in which organized interests shape educational governance and classroom political socialization. Using cross-national data on political mobilization and educational ideology, we estimate the effects of successful nonviolent campaigns on nationalist, socialist-communist, and democratic ideological emphasis within classroom instruction. We find that successful nonviolent campaigns are associated with declines in nationalist and socialist-communist ideological emphasis alongside increased emphasis on democratic norms and democratic institutions. We do not interpret these shifts as movement from indoctrination to ideological neutrality. Rather, following recent work on political socialization and educational ideology, we treat all educational systems as engaged in ideological transmission and interpret the findings as shifts in the ideological orientation emphasized within educational practice. The results suggest that successful nonviolent mobilization is associated with broader political and institutional realignment that reshapes educational political socialization. Parallel estimates for successful violent campaigns do not display the same consistent pattern, although this contrast is descriptive rather than a direct test of the difference between campaign types.
k: nonviolent resistance; political mobilization; ideology in education; political socialization; classroom teaching; education governance; nationalist ideology; democratic norms; ideological transmission; political realignment

t: ŠTO POKREĆE SVIJEST O ODRŽIVOM TURIZMU KOD GENERACIJE Z? EKONOMSKA, EKOLOŠKA I DRUŠTVENA OSVIJEŠTENOST MEĐU MLADIM PORTUGALSKIM PUTNICIMA
a: SAŽETAK: Ovo istraživanje propituje kako ekonomska, ekološka i društvena osviještenost o održivosti zajedno oblikuju svijest o održivom turizmu među članovima generacije Z i funkcionira li taj proces putem iskustvenih mehanizama.Temeljem podataka dobivenih anketiranjem 317 portugalskih putnika u dobi od 14 do 25 godina, testiran je integrirani model pomoću Modeliranja strukturnih jednadžbi metodom parcijalnih najmanjih kvadrata (PLS-SEM).Rezultati pokazuju da se ekonomska svijest pojavljuje kao najutjecajniji izravni pokretač osviještenosti o održivom turizmu.Svijest o okolišu posebno je važna za povećanje zadovoljstva posjetitelja i podržava percepciju lokalnog sudjelovanja.Društvena svijest pozitivno doprinosi kako zadovoljstvu tako i lokalnom sudjelovanju, iako s umjerenijim učinkom.Važno je da i zadovoljstvo posjetitelja i percipirano lokalno sudjelovanje jačaju svijest o održivom turizmu, pri čemu potonje ima središnju ulogu u povezivanju uvjerenja vezanih uz održivost s ukupnom sviješću.
k: Generation Z; economic consciousness; environmental awareness; social awareness; tourist satisfaction; young tourists; Portuguese tourists

t: A Word of WARN-ing: Advance Notice of Layoffs and Labor Market Outcomes
a: This study investigates the impact of state-level Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Acts on advance notice and post-displacement labor market outcomes for U.S. workers from 1993 to 2019. State WARN adoption increases the likelihood of receiving 30+ days of notice by about 4 percentage points. Instrumental variables estimates, supplemented with local average response functions to address weak instruments, show that lengthy notice reduces immediate joblessness by 4 to 7 percentage points. The effects are most pronounced for low-skill workers. Longer term outcomes are less robust. The results indicate that enforceable mandates improve short run transitions, particularly for vulnerable workers.
k: Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act; job displacement; unemployment; labor market outcomes; low-skilled workers; vulnerable workers; job transitions

journal: Journal of Accounting, Ethics and Public Policy
t: From Awareness to Action: Operationalizing Accounting Ethics
a: Accounting programs operate under a recurring tension: AACSB outcomes and IFAC IES 4 require evidence of ethics learning, but curricular integration often lacks the instructional mechanisms to produce such evidence. This study examines a four-component instructional sequence, E⁴P (Exposure, Engagement, Enactment, and Partnership), and the assurance-of-learning artifacts it generates. The paper combines an integrative scoping review with a course-embedded pilot in Accounting Information Systems (n=121) to test a mechanism-aligned measurement suite comprising ethical sensitivity vignettes, DIT-style reasoning, the Hurtt skepticism scale, and a Giving Voice to Values (GVV) performance rubric. The instruments are organized through a Measurement and Scoring Framework that specifies constructs, scoring rubrics, mastery thresholds, and archivable artifacts suitable for assurance-of-learning review. Within the pilot setting, skepticism shifts modestly over a single term, while ethical sensitivity and GVV-rehearsed enactment show larger short-run gains. The paper interprets these patterns as within-student movement consistent with the E⁴P sequence, not as evidence of durable trait change or institution-wide effectiveness, and identifies the conditions under which such artifacts can support accreditation review across courses.
k: accounting ethics education; assurance of learning; ethical sensitivity; Giving Voice to Values; skepticism; accreditation evaluation

t: Reliance on AI in augmented strategic decision-making: Navigating cultural and national dynamics
a: While AI tools are available worldwide, the institutional context in which decision-makers operate likely influences their reliance on this technology. Our study examines how national institutional environments shape managers’ reliance on AI tools in augmented strategic decisions. We investigate the role of collective norms shaped by two institutions—national culture and the national government—on AI augmented strategic decision-making. We conducted a vignette study with 172 managers across seven countries. Following the theory of cultural tightness and looseness, we show that cultural tightness increases decision-makers' reliance on AI. Additionally, in tighter cultures, where individuals internalize hierarchically defined norms and rules, government AI endorsement further strengthens reliance on AI advice. We contribute to the literature on AI-human interaction and on cross-cultural decision-making by showing how different cultural environments can either enhance or hinder managerial reliance on AI, while also bringing important implications for MNEs and governments seeking to leverage AI for competitive advantage.
k: AI reliance; national culture; institutional environment; cross-cultural decision making; human-AI interaction; management decision-making; multinational corporations; competitive advantage

journal: Electronic Journal of Information Systems in Developing Countries
t: Digitization and Productivity in Senegalese SMEs : An Examination of Internal Structural Factors
a: The effects of digitization in small and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs) vary, even when resources are available. Success depends not only on resource availability but also on how effectively these resources are used, by analyzing the mechanisms that drive these effects and integrating them within the business. This study investigates how different forms of internal capital, as strategic resources, influence the digitization process and the productivity of Senegalese SMEs. This includes technological capital, general and specific human capital, infrastructure, and organizational capital, and their impact on the adoption and use of digital tools in SMEs. A quantitative cross‐sectional design was employed, with a structured questionnaire to assess the perceptions of 255 respondents, comprising managers and employees, from 120 SMEs across multiple sectors in Senegal about digital technology adoption and its impact on productivity. Principal component analysis and multiple regression were used to analyze relationships among variables. The findings highlight that digitization positively influences the productivity of Senegalese SMEs, with each internal factor playing a significant role. A bootstrapped mediation analysis nevertheless indicates that digitization does not mediate the relationship between internal resources and productivity: once resource endowments are held constant, the indirect path through digitization is not significant. The results show that effectively integrating internal resources supports digitization and improves organizational performance. Theoretically, this study adds to the literature on digitization and SME performance in Africa by testing an integrated explanatory model in which digitization is positioned as the mechanism linking internal resources to productivity, and by showing that this mediating role is not supported in the Senegalese SME context. From a managerial perspective, digitization should be part of the firm's overall strategy rather than seen only as a technical solution. Aligning digital initiatives with long‐term objectives can lead to substantial improvements in performance and competitiveness.
k: digitization; small and medium-sized enterprises; productivity; internal capital; technological capital; human capital; organizational capital; infrastructure; digital technology adoption; firm performance; Senegal; digital strategy

t: When Communications Fail and Values Clash: What Drives Employees to Resist Information Security Compliance?
a: As internal data breaches pose growing threats, understanding the psychological drivers of employee compliance with information security (IS) policies is crucial. Drawing on person–environment fit and value congruence theory, this study examines how communication uncertainty, communication ambiguity, and value dissimilarity impact IS-related anxiety—distinguishing between prospective and inhibitory dimensions—and how such anxiety reduces compliance intention. Survey data from 397 employees reveal that unclear or ambiguous IS communication heightens both forms of anxiety, which subsequently undermines compliance. Prospective anxiety stems from future-oriented concerns, while inhibitory anxiety arises from confusion or paralysis in the present. Moreover, value dissimilarity amplifies these anxiety effects, indicating that misaligned IS values intensify employees’ psychological reactivity to communication breakdowns. These findings contribute theoretically by identifying dual anxiety pathways linking communication to compliance and highlighting value dissimilarity as a critical contextual moderator. Practically, the study emphasizes the need for clear communication and value congruence to support secure behavior.
k: information security policy compliance; communication uncertainty; person-environment fit

t: Well-being drivers for immigrant and native-born entrepreneurs: The effects of competence and relatedness
a: Entrepreneur well-being has attracted increasing attention among academics and practitioners as scholars have called for broadening the entrepreneurship outcomes beyond financial considerations, and practitioners have had to cope with increased stressors and challenges amid global economic and social uncertainty. However, little is known about differences in well-being drivers for different groups of entrepreneurs. Drawing on self-determination theory, we use data from the Canadian Index of Well-being ( N = 655) and compare how competence and relatedness affect the well-being of immigrant versus native-born entrepreneurs. The evidence demonstrates the differential ways in which these dimensions affect well-being with competence being critical for native-born entrepreneurs, while relatedness is more important to immigrant entrepreneurs. The findings illustrate the need for considering the contextual embeddedness of entrepreneurial activities for a better understanding of the factors that drive well-being for diverse groups of entrepreneurs.
k: entrepreneurial well-being; immigrant entrepreneurs; competence; relatedness; self-determination theory; contextual embeddedness

journal: International Journal of Entrepreneurship and Small Business
t: Financial literacy, attitude, and knowledge as the predictors of firm performance of SME owners in Bangladesh
a: The fundamental objective of this study is to investigate the mediating effects of financial attitude and knowledge on the relationship between financial literacy and firm performance of SME owners in Bangladesh. Using the convenience sampling technique, we collected the data from a total of 317 owners of SMEs from eight divisions in Bangladesh. The findings revealed that financial literacy, attitude, and knowledge significantly impact firm performance. Besides, financial attitude and knowledge partially mediate the relationship between financial literacy and firm performance. This research has significant implications for SME owners as these findings motivate them to develop their financial literacy, positive attitude, and knowledge that are positively related to better firm performance.
k: financial literacy; financial attitude; financial knowledge; firm performance; small and medium-sized enterprises; SME owners; mediating effect; Bangladesh

t: Can FinTech innovate green finance? Scrutinising the financial ecologies and innovation dynamics of FinTech for forest restoration
a: Green finance has struggled to make a difference in climate change mitigation. For some, the main limitations lie in scaling and diversifying financial flows and instruments to close the climate funding gap, while for others, green finance is fundamentally flawed as an incumbent-led project that opens new environmental frontiers for accumulation. In response, FinTech has been touted as offering the technological solutions that could both bridge the climate financing gap and disrupt the systemic issues green finance faces. Yet, critical voices question whether FinTech is simply the latest ‘technological turn’ in a long line of socioecological fixes, designed to reintermediate financial activity onto increasingly powerful FinTech platforms. To assess the potential for FinTech to innovate green finance, we explore a suite of FinTech innovations aimed at enticing, incentivising, and thus mobilising retail consumers to fund tree planting for forest restoration as a means of delivering climate, biodiversity, and livelihood outcomes. Rooted in the award-winning Ant Forest innovation by Alibaba, we document eight subsequent variations of the Ant Forest model by different FinTech firms, who share the same focus on enabling consumer-funded tree planting – but modify the initial innovation in various ways. By utilising a ‘platform ecologies’ framework, we reveal that these innovations have delivered significant environmental outputs , with these nine FinTechs collectively financing the planting of over 750 million trees, but that evidence of environmental impact in terms of tree survival and carbon sequestration rates, remains vague. Moreover, whilst these nine FinTechs offer novel green finance solutions, they are also fundamentally driven by platform development to increase users and revenue – rather than environmental concern.
k: fintech; green finance; forest restoration; tree planting; Ant Forest; Alibaba; platform ecology; carbon sequestration; tree survival; financial intermediation; livelihoods

t: Metastability for the Curie–Weiss–Potts model with unbounded random interactions
a: We analyse the metastable behaviour of the disordered Curie–Weiss–Potts (DCWP) model subject to a Glauber dynamics. The model is a randomly disordered version of the mean-field q-spin Potts model (CWP), where the interaction coefficients between spins are general independent random variables. These random variables are chosen to have fixed mean (for simplicity taken to be 1) and well defined cumulant generating function, with a fixed distribution not depending on the number of particles. The system evolves as a discrete-time Markov chain with single spin flip Metropolis dynamics at finite inverse temperature β. We provide a comparison of the metastable behaviour of the CWP and DCWP models, when N→∞. First, we establish the metastability of the CWP model and, using this result, prove metastability for the DCWP model (with high probability). We then determine the ratio between the metastable transition time for the DCWP model and the corresponding time for the CWP model. Specifically, we derive the asymptotic tail behavior and moments of this ratio. Our proof combines the potential-theoretic approach to metastability with concentration of measure techniques, the latter adapted to our specific context.
k: metastability; Glauber dynamics; Metropolis dynamics; concentration of measure; cumulant generating function

journal: Journal of Comparative Policy Analysis: research and practice
t: Central–Local Government Relationship, Digital Technology, and Property Tax Administration in Developing Countries: A Comparative Analysis of the Ghanaian Case
a: Property tax is recognised as a crucial financial tool for local governments to support development initiatives. Its administration – that is, the identification, valuing, taxing, and collecting revenue from real property within a jurisdiction – however, remains problematic. Recently, some scholars have asserted that this problem can be resolved through the introduction of technology, which many governments have now adopted. Unfortunately, the problems of property tax administration (PTA) continue to persist. This persistence can be attributed to the relationship between central and local governments, where the former keeps constraining the latter’s ability to function as the administrators of property tax through omissions and commissions. Using Ghana as a case study, the article asks: How does the central–local government relationship impact PTA in developing countries despite the introduction of technology in this endeavour? From a political economy perspective, the article argues that the persistence of this issue stems from the failure to examine tension in the central–local government relationship and how it affects PTA. It proposes ways to resolve the tension between the two levels of government.
k: property tax administration; central-local government relations; digital technologies; local government finance; fiscal decentralization; political economy of taxation; real property valuation; tax collection; Ghana

t: How AR Shapes Buying Intention: Mood, Cognition, and a Multi-Analytical Perspective Using PLS-SEM, MGA, NCA, and fsQCA
a: Augmented reality (AR) helps customers feel more confident in online shopping; however, the mechanisms of behavior through AR are still not fully understood. This study proposes an Affective Goal-Driven Technology Acceptance Framework (AGTAF) to explain AR features leading to continuous usage intention (CUI) and online purchase intention (OPI). Data were collected from 956 respondents who were randomly assigned to use one of three AR applications, such as Lesslens, Room Planner, or Wanna Kicks. The results demonstrate the important role of CUI, the moderating role of mood, and the configurations of variables through the combination of various methods such as PLS-SEM, MGA, NCA, and fsQCA. Theoretically, the study proposes the AGTAF by integrating technological, cognitive, and affective dimensions with online purchase intention. Practically, we propose managerial implications to optimize AR design and encourage users to shop more in modern online retailing.
k: augmented reality; online purchase intention; continuous usage intention; mood; technology acceptance; online shopping; AR application design; online retail; consumer behavior

t: The effect of consumers’ power states on pay-what-you-want pricing
a: Based on the agentic–communal model of power, this study explores the influence and internal mechanism of consumers’ power states on pay-what-you-want pricing. Although prior research has offered foundational insights into customer behavior in pay-what-you-want contexts, many of the identified factors lack generalizability across different contexts. To address this limitation, the present study integrates both personal and social perspectives by examining power states as a central factor. The results show that individuals with a high sense of power pay less than individuals with a low sense of power in pay-what-you-want contexts and that the agentic–communal orientation mediates the effect of power states on the payment. Furthermore, when social motivation is salient, individuals with a high sense of power pay more and the payment difference between low-power and high-power individuals decreases. The findings not only contribute to the literature by deepening the understanding of how power states influence consumer behavior and identifying key antecedents of pay-what-you-want pricing decisions, but also provides a theoretical reference for marketers to formulate more targeted marketing strategies and improve marketing performance based on pay-what-you-want pricing.
k: pay-what-you-want pricing; social motivation; consumer payment behavior

t: Reputational Damage and Stigmatisation of South African Government Departments, State-Owned Enterprises and NPOs: Are Corrective Measures Going to Help?
a: Over the past two decades, South Africa has experienced pervasive fraud and corruption on an unprecedented scale. The reputational damage and organisational stigmatisation arising from large-scale corruption within government departments, state-owned enterprises, and non-profit organisations have prompted the establishment of several presidential commissions of inquiry aimed at uncovering and investigating these criminal activities. The findings of these commissions have revealed deeply troubling and systemic practices. Consequently, a significant challenge facing many public institutions and non-profit organisations is whether they possess the capacity to address the extent of the criminal conduct, implement meaningful institutional reforms, and ultimately restore public trust and legitimacy.
k: reputational damage; corruption; fraud; public sector institutions; state-owned enterprises; nonprofit organizations; institutional reform; public trust; legitimacy; South Africa

t: Unlocking AI's potential in accounting: A study on adoption barriers and drivers
a: Accountants play a vital role in driving the implementation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to improve financial analysis and performance measurement, but their readiness to adopt the technology is uneven. Drawing on the dual-factor model, this research examines the barriers and drivers to AI adoption. Barriers include knowledge and use of Excel-based data analytics (DA). Drivers include AI training, adoption of DA tools, and accountants' initiatives aimed at reducing resistance to technological change. These factors explain how accountants can suffer from status quo bias that prevents them from adopting AI and how the bias can be alleviated by organizational efforts. We conducted a survey on 271 accounting professionals and used descriptive analysis and Poisson regression to empirically test the effects of the factors. The results demonstrate the significant impacts of these factors on AI adoption. This study advances the literature on AI adoption by providing new insights into the barriers and drivers regarding its adoption in corporate environments.
k: artificial intelligence adoption; accountants; dual-factor model; technology adoption barriers; technology adoption factors; data analytics; AI training; resistance to technology; status quo bias; information technology in accounting

t: Economic Integration in MENA: The Global, Regional, and Subregional Integration Indices and Their Dynamic Interactions
a: We propose a new index based on the gravity model to measure global, regional, and subregional economic integration. Europe, America, Asia, and MENA exhibit different dynamic interactions between these three levels of integration. The MENA region has a distinctive dumbbell integration pattern - strong at the global and subregional levels but weak at the regional level. The panel data cointegration approach reveals that different types of integration are complements but not substitutes. Regional integration has the strongest positive externality in terms of fostering other types of integration. Promoting regionalization is the most efficient policy option.
k: economic integration; Middle East and North Africa; gravity model; regional integration; subregional integration; global integration; regionalization policy

t: Pay‐for‐prominence: The (un)intended consequences of monetary incentives on employees' networks and attrition
a: Research Summary We introduce the concept of pay‐for‐prominence , a system where employees are monetarily incentivized to become knowledge hubs in the intrafirm network and examine its effects on employees' networks and attrition. Integrating social network theory with relational incentives theory, we argue that pay‐for‐prominence motivates strategic networking behaviors that lead to the emergence of prominent connectors. However, these changes are associated with higher attrition as employees are preoccupied with networking, thus suggesting a trade‐off between enhanced connectivity in the short term and the risk of network fragmentation in the long term. Using a field quasi‐experiment in a multinational firm, we show that organizations can successfully incentivize employees' network prominence, but doing so may produce unintended consequences. Managerial Summary We examine the impact of using monetary incentives to encourage employees to become knowledge hubs in the workplace informal network—a term we label pay‐for‐prominence. We find that offering monetary rewards based on network metrics encourages employees to broaden their connections, enhancing knowledge flows within the firm. However, employees who become more socially prominent experience higher attrition than those who do not, as they become preoccupied with networking. Therefore, while incentivizing networking can improve knowledge sharing, it also requires careful management to avoid unintended consequences, such as the exit of key players that could cause fragmentation of the social network. Managers should weigh the benefits of increased connectivity against the risks of fragmentation when designing incentive programs aimed at fostering informal networks.
k: financial incentives; employee networks; employee attrition; knowledge hub; knowledge sharing; network fragmentation; strategic networking; organizational incentives

journal: International Journal of Trade and Global Markets
t: Accountability in the workplace: analysing the employees perception in different cultural contexts
a: Accountability involves employees taking responsibility for their actions, decisions, and outcomes, aligning individual efforts with organisational goals. It fosters ethical decision-making, proactive problem-solving, and workplace democracy while enhancing motivation and performance. Organisationally, it ensures resource efficiency, goal achievement, and a strong reputation. Given cultural variations in accountability perceptions, this study examines how cultural differences in China, Russia, and Italy shape employees' views. Using quantitative and qualitative data from an online survey, the study provides insights for managers fostering accountability in diverse settings.
k: accountability; employee perceptions; cultural differences; cross-cultural comparison; China; Russia; Italy; workplace ethics; organizational performance; workplace democracy; employee motivation

t: Value for money in public procurement in Tanzania – an outcome of accountability as a governance tool
a: Purpose The aim of this study was to establish the relationship between accountability as a pillar of public procurement and achievement of value for money in the context of Tanzania as fostered by Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) 16 to engage fairness in the conduct of society. Design/methodology/approach This study adopted a cross-sectional survey design using 270 respondents purposively selected from 14 Local Government Authorities (LGA) in four regions of Tanzania. The data were analysed quantitatively using the Covariance-Based Structural Equation Modelling (CB-SEM). Findings The results revealed that there is a strong and significant relationship between accountability and value for money. Research limitations/implications The study recommends that LGAs have a clear chain of responsibilities for both public officers and contractors of projects. Based on SDG number 16 of a fairer society under the National Implementation Strategy of Tanzania using target 16, the study recommends that bureaucratic approvals should be reduced because involvement of too many people makes it difficult to hold people accountable in case of any wrongdoing. Practical implications Public procuring entities in Tanzania should strengthen the lines of accountability in public procurement to achieve value for money and hence good governance. Originality/value The study contributes to the multidisciplinary growing debate on good governance in public procurement and the attainment of value for money as fostered by SDG under the National Implementation Strategy of Tanzania as per target 16.6. Also, the study contributes to the public value theory on how it is applied in the local context of Tanzania.
k: value for money; public procurement; accountability; good governance; SDG 16; local government authority; public value; Tanzania

t: Wearable ankle activity monitor overestimates energy expenditure during ecological walking tasks in individuals with stroke and healthy adults
a: Assessment of physical activity intensity is essential for guiding rehabilitation after stroke. Wearable activity monitors are used to estimate energy expenditure during walking; however, their validity in stroke populations under real-life walking conditions remains uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the validity of an ActiGraph GT3X for estimating energy expenditure during walking tasks in stroke survivors using indirect calorimetry as the reference method. Thirty stroke survivors and 30 healthy controls performed indoor and outdoor walking tasks, including overground walking, stair ascent and descent, irregular terrain walking, and uphill and downhill walking. Energy expenditure expressed in metabolic equivalents was measured using the ActiGraph GT3X worn at the ankle and a portable gas exchange analyzer. Agreement between methods was assessed using Bland-Altman analyses and linear regression models. The ActiGraph GT3X overestimated energy expenditure across most walking tasks in both groups, with percentage differences ranging from 25.7 to 112% in stroke survivors and from 18.1 to 149.1% in healthy controls. In stroke survivors, walking speed was significantly associated with the difference in energy expenditure (ActiGraph GT3X - indirect calorimetry) across most tasks, with higher speeds leading to greater overestimation (e.g. β = 9.01, P < 0.001, R2 = 0.41 for stair descent). In healthy controls, this association was observed only for selected tasks, including overground walking and stair descent. These findings indicate that the ActiGraph GT3X has limited validity for energy expenditure estimation during ecological walking tasks. Although the device may provide relative indicators of effort, its outputs should be interpreted with caution.
k: wearable activity trackers; ActiGraph GT3X+; energy expenditure estimation; stroke survivors; walking; measurement validity; indirect calorimetry; walking speed; stair climbing; uphill and downhill walking; physical activity intensity; stroke rehabilitation

t: From Employment Exit to Occupational Reallocation: Child Penalties in Vietnam*
a: This study provides new evidence on the magnitude, heterogeneity and mechanisms of the child penalties in Vietnam. Using Labour Force Survey data (2010–2020) and a pseudo‐event study design, we focus on working‐age individuals who experienced their first childbirth between ages 20 and 45. Guided by a conceptual framework, we examine the extent to which child penalties are associated with labour supply responses and job reallocation, as opposed to within‐job adjustments, and how these patterns are moderated by individual, household and institutional factors. The results show that mothers' earnings decline by approximately 35 per cent at first childbirth, while fathers experience a small, statistically insignificant increase of approximately three per cent. This gap narrows over time, leaving an 18.3 per cent relative decline in mothers' earnings after 10 years. Initial losses reflect immediate employment exits, whereas long‐run patterns are consistent with reallocation towards lower‐paying and less formal jobs, with little change in hours worked. Penalties are smaller among mothers with only one child and those with greater family and institutional support. Furthermore, education plays a central role, shaping both labour supply and occupational mobility. These findings highlight the importance of policies that support continuous employment and mitigate occupational reallocation to alleviate child penalties in Vietnam.
k: child penalty; first birth; employment exit; labor supply; working-age women; Vietnam; family support; job mobility

t: The Lost Futures of Gender Diversity in STEM: Developing a diffractive methodology to study acts of disappearance
a: Gender segregation in STEM labour markets remains a problem despite the immense attention to the issue in recent years. This article studies diversity initiatives aiming to amend the lack of women in STEM by helping girls and young women to develop STEM career aspirations. Inspired by Karen Barad, we develop a novel diffractive methodology designed to address the intricate acts of disappearance through which knowledge, identities, and experiences are made absent from organisational realities. We demonstrate this methodology by reading Danish STEM diversity initiatives diffractively through taxidermied animal specimens. This allows us to identify the practices through which gender diversity disappear and show how harmful gender stereotypes are reproduced within the very attempts to counter them. Thus, the contribution of the article is two-fold: We offer a novel methodology apt to encounter and engage with absences and to experiment with the new meanings that can emerge when what has been erased is re-introduced into the analysis. Moreover, we show that despite well-meaning intentions and substantial funding, contemporary diversity initiatives cannot be expected to push beyond or transgress the current constraints on viable gendered identities in STEM.
k: gender diversity in STEM; gender segregation; diversity initiatives; women in STEM; STEM career aspirations; diffractive methodology; Karen Barad; gender stereotypes; taxidermy; gendered identity; organisational practices

t: Electronic Invoicing and Digital Reporting: The State of Play in Spain in 2026
a: E-invoicing and digital reporting are a worldwide trend. In this article, the author depicts the current state of play in Spain of legislation introducing mandatory e-invoicing and digital reporting of invoice content. The author explains the three pieces of legislation in Spain dealing with these digital trends, which have different levels of maturity. He concludes the analysis by offering self-produced conclusions and recommendations about the opportunities and challenges for Spain of the adoption of these three initiatives, highlighting the need to prevent overlapping of obligations and double reporting and the requirement for alignment with the ViDA package by July 2030.
k: electronic invoicing; digital reporting; VAT law; Spanish tax law

t: Does halal destination designation matter on domestic tourist trips? Evidence from Indonesian provinces
a: Purpose In Indonesia, where most of the population is Muslim, the designation of halal tourism destinations is expected to shape domestic tourism patterns. Rather than assessing halal service features directly, this study aims to examine whether policy-level recognition as a halal destination is associated with increased domestic tourist trips. Design/methodology/approach Using panel data from 34 Indonesian provinces spanning 2016–2024, the study applies a difference-in-differences (DID) framework with province and year fixed effects. The model controls the impact of COVID-19, population size and per capita income. As a robustness check, the analysis also compares pre- and post-COVID periods and includes OLS and random effects estimations. Findings The results show that halal-designated provinces recorded significantly higher domestic tourist trips, particularly before the pandemic, indicating that policy-level branding can effectively influence domestic travel. During and after the COVID-19 pandemic, the incremental effect of halal designation on overall domestic tourist trips did not significantly change, suggesting that its relative advantage remained stable over time. Research limitations/implications While the DID design provides meaningful comparisons, it is constrained by the absence of pre-2016 data, which limits the ability to fully establish parallel trends. Originality/value This study contributes to the halal tourism literature by shifting the analytical focus from international markets toward domestic mobility and the branding effects of policy recognition in a Muslim-majority context.
k: halal tourism; domestic tourism; tourist trips; destination branding; tourism policy; COVID-19 pandemic impact; Muslim-majority countries; Indonesian provinces

t: Teaching Tip: Generative AI in Education: Building Intelligent Tutors With Large Language Models
a: The increasing power of computers in education drove the evolution of one-size-fits-all computer-assisted instruction systems to intelligent tutoring systems that offer individualized learning experiences. The emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence, particularly large language models, has enabled a new era of intelligent tutoring. This paper presents a practical approach to building an SQL tutor using a Generative Artificial Intelligence chatbot, demonstrating how instructors can easily leverage Generative Artificial Intelligence to deliver personalized, context-aware instruction. Through carefully engineered prompts, the tutor guides students with adaptive feedback, mimicking the behavior of a skilled human instructor. We detail the design process, share student interaction data, and evaluate the tutor’s effectiveness based on survey responses and comparative performance analysis. Our findings suggest that Generative Artificial Intelligence-based tutors can significantly enhance learning outcomes and offer scalable, low-cost solutions for educators. In addition to presenting complete details of and experience with a tutor for a specific topic, the paper provides guidance for instructors to leverage the underlying framework to develop domain-specific Generative Artificial Intelligence-enabled tutors for other topics, thereby contributing to the growing body of research on AI-enhanced education.
k: generative AI in education; large language models; intelligent tutoring systems; chatbots; prompt engineering; adaptive feedback; personalized learning; computer-assisted instruction; student interaction data

t: Interactions Among Non‐Disabled Employees at a Special‐Purpose Subsidiary from the Perspective of Non‐Disabled Subordinates
a: In this paper, with regard to the process of social interactions between non‐disabled managers and non‐disabled subordinates at a special‐purpose subsidiary: (a) We move our analysis from the managers' side (Ohshima & Takeshita, 2025) to the subordinate side. We discover regularities of events from the subordinate side, including cognitive factors affecting the attitude of the subordinates, which were not obtained in the managerial analysis. (b) By comparing this analysis with the analysis performed on the managers' side and discovering core categories, we aimed to increase the level of abstraction of theory and to obtain more general suggestions. We conducted semi‐structured interviews with 11 general employees (five males, six females) and analyzed the data using a grounded theory approach. The results revealed: (a) regularities that shape the attitudes of non‐disabled subordinates, including factors not visible to managers, and the qualitative characteristics of distinct stages (Stage A: Trial‐and‐error approach; Stage B: Parallel relationship; Stage B´: Strengthening the cooperative system); and (b) the core category “Dimensions of Role and Value.” These findings suggest that adopting a “non‐disabled vs. non‐disabled” perspective—re‐examining how managers and non‐disabled subordinates interact within the framework of workplace inclusion—is essential.
k: workplace inclusion; employment of people with disabilities; social interaction; cognitive factors

journal: European Journal of Transport and Infrastructure Research
t: Household preferences regarding residential location and commuter choices, depending on household type and teleworking options
a: Residential location choices and travel behaviour have implications for sustainability. For example, preferences for detached single-family homes in a green environment may lead to longer commutes, mostly by car. In the face of environmental challenges, commuting is essential for developing strategies for a more sustainable future. At the same time, it remains uncertain how commuting distances, car use for commuting, and urbanisation trends will evolve in the future. This study focuses on understanding individual choices and the relationship between residential, work and commuting choices for different household types. It is based on a quantitative online survey of residential location and mode choices of commuters in Germany using discrete choice experiments. The results show that travel time values are significantly lower for teleworkers than for non-teleworkers. Regarding mode choice, walking is perceived more negatively by family households, young households are most sensitive to car travel time, and public transport seems less attractive to them. In general, in a teleworking scenario, the elements of public transport use that are currently perceived as burdensome (especially waiting time) become less important. In terms of modal shift, telework could reduce car use for young households, but not for family households. This study provides an insight into the relationship between residential location, commuting and mode choice and opens a discussion on the impact of teleworking on the sustainability of commuting.
k: residential location choice; remote work; household types; value of travel time; car use; public transport; walking; modal shift; sustainable commuting; family households; young households; waiting time; urbanization

t: A Fourier-Based Inference Method for Learning Interaction Kernels in Particle Systems
a: We consider the problem of inferring the interaction kernel of stochastic interacting particle systems from observations of a single particle. We adopt a semiparametric approach and represent the interaction kernel in terms of a generalized Fourier series. The basis functions in this expansion are tailored to the problem at hand and are chosen to be orthogonal polynomials with respect to the invariant measure of the mean-field dynamics. The generalized Fourier coefficients are obtained as the solution of an appropriate linear system whose coefficients depend on the moments of the invariant measure, and which are approximated from the particle trajectory that we observe. We quantify the approximation error in the Lebesgue space weighted by the invariant measure and study the asymptotic properties of the estimator in the joint limit as the observation interval and the number of particles tend to infinity, i.e., the joint large time–mean-field limit. We also explore the regime where an increasing number of generalized Fourier coefficients are needed to represent the interaction kernel. Our theoretical results are supported by extensive numerical simulations.
k: interacting particle systems; generalized Fourier series; orthogonal polynomials; invariant measures; mean-field limit; semiparametric estimation; approximation error

t: How connectivity in online social interactions influence the loyalty and WOM toward games? The role of need to belong
a: Purpose This paper aims to analyze the role of social interactions in free-to-play online games, specifically examining how connectivity influences player loyalty and word-of-mouth (WOM) regarding micro-transaction behaviors. A key purpose is to investigate the moderating effect of the Need to Belong, hypothesizing that it amplifies the positive impact of connectivity on these crucial player outcomes. The study seeks to deepen the understanding of social dynamics driving player behavior in online gaming communities. Design/methodology/approach The authors conducted quantitative, descriptive research with a non-probabilistic sample of 235 free-to-play online mobile game players. Participants were recruited via email and WhatsApp and signed consent forms. The survey included sociodemographic questions, gaming habits and measures of connectivity (Hsiao and Chen, 2016), Need to Belong (Leary et al., 2013), loyalty (Yang and Peterson, 2004) and WOM (Hegner et al., 2017). Scales were adapted for Brazilian respondents using double-back translation (Douglas and Graig, 2007). After a pilot test with 12 Business Administration students, data were collected and analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, EFA, CFA and regression models (Anderson and Gerbing, 1988). Findings This study expands social capital theory by integrating the belongingness hypothesis to explore the synergistic effects of connectivity and the need to belong in online gaming. The results confirm that connectivity significantly and positively influences both player loyalty and word-of-mouth. Crucially, the Need to Belong was found to significantly amplify these relationships, demonstrating its vital moderating role as players seek validation and emotional connections within gaming communities. These findings highlight the critical role of social and emotional dynamics in virtual environments, offering a deeper understanding of how social interactions drive player behavior and the repurchase of virtual goods. Research limitations/implications This study focuses on free-to-play games, limiting generalizability to other monetization models such as subscription-based games. Future research should examine whether similar social interaction mechanisms apply in these contexts. The data primarily captures short-term behaviors; longitudinal studies are needed to explore how social interactions evolve and impact long-term player retention. Individual differences, such as personality, culture and gaming experience, should also be investigated as potential moderators of connectivity effects. Finally, reliance on self-reported data may introduce bias; incorporating objective in-game data and exploring emerging technologies such as virtual reality and augmented reality can enhance the understanding of social connectivity in gaming. Practical implications Game developers should implement strategies that enhance connectivity and a sense of belonging among players to boost loyalty and word-of-
k: online social interaction; connectivity; need to belong; player loyalty; word of mouth; free-to-play games; in-game purchases; social capital theory; online gaming communities; virtual goods; player retention; mobile games; moderating effect; player behavior; game monetization; player engagement; player satisfaction

t: Relationship Between Social Connectedness and Quality of Life in Older Adults: An Examination of Sex Differences
a: BACKGROUND: Despite the literature supporting the important role of social connectedness in older people's Quality of Life (QoL), study of this association has been scarce, especially sex-specific social mechanisms. This study aimed to examine how social connectedness related to QoL in community-dwelling older adults, considering sex differences. METHOD: 709 people from Spain, aged 60 and over participated in the study and completed a survey that included sociodemographic characteristics, social connectedness, psychological resources, mental health and QoL. Path analysis was performed to test the hypothesized model. Associations between the assessed variables were tested separately for men and women. RESULTS: The relationship between family function and QoL was fully mediated by psychological resources and mental health, but the direct paths used by women were different from men. The relation between loneliness and QoL was partially mediated, with gratitude and resilience playing a more prominent role among women. CONCLUSIONS: The critical role of social factors is highlighted, as humans are inherently social beings. The study found sex differences in the relationship between social connectedness and QoL, mediated by psychological resources, well-being, and distress. Men and women cope with adversity differently. It is important to consider sex differences when designing interventions for older adults.
k: social connectedness; quality of life; older adults; sex differences; loneliness; family functions; psychological resources; gratitude; resilience; mental health; community-dwelling older adults

t: Cross-border portfolio ownership and endogenous tax-system divergence under origin taxation
a: This paper examines endogenous choice between ad valorem and specific commodity taxation under the origin principle when residents hold portfolio equity in foreign producers. Although allocation-equivalent instruments implement the same effective marginal cost, they divide operating surplus differently between domestic tax revenue and after-tax profit. Foreign ownership therefore creates an allocation-conditional incidence wedge: with positive operating surplus, a positive ad valorem tax has a higher national value than its specific counterpart, while the ranking reverses for subsidies. This result applies to arbitrary deterministic segmented demands and does not rely on linearity or market symmetry. In the two-stage system-and-rate game, however, governments compare continuation values because a system change induces both rates to adjust. A common institutional disadvantage of ad valorem taxation can make system choices strategic substitutes; when the direct ownership-incidence effect dominates strategic rate feedback, ownership asymmetry can then select which country adopts which system. A numerically verified linear benchmark yields a unique asymmetric subgame-perfect equilibrium in which the country with greater inward foreign ownership adopts a positive ad valorem tax and the other adopts a positive specific tax. Thus ownership selects the direction of differentiation rather than generating it without a countervailing institutional force. The ownership variable is passive resident portfolio ownership, not strategic corporate cross-holdings.
k: ad valorem taxation; tax incidence; operating surplus; strategic substitutes; subgame perfect equilibrium; foreign ownership; tax competition

journal: International Journal of Manufacturing Technology and Management
t: Research on automatic planning algorithm of surfacing repair path based on 3D vision technology
a: To solve the problems existing in the traditional automatic planning algorithm of surfacing repair path, an automatic planning algorithm of surfacing repair path based on 3D vision technology is proposed. Firstly, the one-way planning distance is calculated, the pixel value containing weld in the target image is set to 0 based on 3D vision technology, the threshold value of weld is calculated, the surfacing repair path planning target is constructed, and the planning nodes are set. The, calculate the displacement value of the component that needs welding deformation, and get the automatic planning result of surfacing repair path. The experimental results show that the target location result obtained by the proposed algorithm is more accurate, and the characteristics of the weld test sample image can be accurately planned. The average root mean square error after the supplement is smaller, which is 0.1 cm, indicating that the proposed method can effectively improve the path planning effect.
k: automatic path planning; 3D vision; weld detection; displacement estimation

journal: Supply Chain Forum: An International Journal
t: Conceptualising Industry 5.0 in Supply Chains: Integrating Human-Centricity, Sustainability, and Ethics
a: Industry 5.0 represents a value-oriented industrial paradigm that moves beyond the technology-driven logic of Industry 4.0 by placing human-centric, sustainability, and ethics at the core of production and supply systems. This study examines how these principles are reflected in logistics and supply chain management through a structured conceptual review. A PRISMA-inspired screening protocol was applied to the Scopus and Web of Science databases covering the period 2015–2025, resulting in the selection of 18 studies for conceptual synthesis. The review identifies three interrelated transformation dimensions shaping Industry 5.0-oriented supply chains: human – machine collaboration, social and environmental sustainability, and ethical, value-based technology governance. Human – machine collaboration connects technology adoption with operational outcomes through mechanisms related to ergonomics, cognitive workload, and employee well-being. Sustainability objectives influence system-level supply chain design and resource allocation decisions, while ethical governance frameworks guide responsible technology use and support managerial accountability and stakeholder trust. By theorising the interactions among these dimensions, the study develops an integrated conceptual framework that explains how value-based priorities reshape logistics and supply chain structures and management practices, and provides a foundation for future empirical research.
k: Industry 5.0; supply chain management; human-machine collaboration; sustainability; ethics; technology governance; human-centricity; employee well-being; mental workload; human factors; supply chain design; stakeholder trust
