t: The generalized Zagreb index for non-plane and plane recursive trees
a: The Zagreb index, which is defined as the sum of squares of degrees of the nodes of a tree, was studied in previous works by martingale techniques for random non-plane recursive trees and classes of random trees which are close to random plane recursive trees. These techniques are not easily amended to the generalized Zagreb index, which is defined similarly but with squares replaced by higher powers. We use the moment-transfer approach to (i) obtain the first-order asymptotics of moments and (ii) prove limit laws for the (suitably normalized) generalized Zagreb index for random non-plane and plane recursive trees. For the former, we show that for all higher powers the limit law is normal; for the latter, we show for cubes and fourth powers that it is a non-normal law.
k: Zagreb indices; random recursive trees; moment transfer; asymptotic moments; limit laws; martingale method

t: The Social Enterprise Brand Success Framework: A Qualitative Study
a: This study explores the critical success factors (CSFs) that contribute to brand growth and sustainability among social enterprises. Focusing on how social enterprises build brands that effectively communicate their hybrid value proposition, balancing social mission with market viability, this research employs the Gioia methodology with 29 in-depth interviews across diverse sectors in India. Findings reveal that social enterprise branding is a multi-dimensional process shaped by four core dimensions: Core Purpose & Impact, Value Proposition & Delivery, Stakeholder Engagement & Communication, and Ecosystem Integration & Legitimacy. These dimensions are interconnected through cross-cutting enablers of Leadership & Culture and Adaptability & Resilience. The study contributes to social entrepreneurship literature by providing a contextually relevant framework for understanding brand success in hybrid organisations. Practical implications include guidance for social enterprise leaders on balancing mission and market in brand development, and for ecosystem builders on supporting effective branding strategies. The research highlights that successful social enterprise branding involves social purpose, authentic engagement, and contextual fit within larger ecosystems, offering a roadmap for building brands that effectively communicate hybrid value propositions in emerging economies.
k: brand success; success factors; stakeholder engagement; ecosystem integration; organizational legitimacy; leadership and organizational culture; brand sustainability; emerging markets

t: Board efficiency index, government ownership and financial performance of Shanghai stock exchange companies
a: Purpose This study investigates the impact of a multidimensional board efficiency index (BEI) on firm financial performance (FP) and examines the moderating role of government ownership (GO) in China’s emerging market. It addresses gaps in prior literature by integrating six board attributes into a holistic governance metric and testing the government influence. Design/methodology/approach Using panel data from 1,226 Shanghai Stock Exchange-listed firms (2018–2022), the study employs a system Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) model to mitigate endogeneity. BEI is constructed by synthesizing board size, independence, CEO duality, meeting frequency, political connections and financial expertise. FP is measured via Economic Value-Added Rate and Tobin’s Q. GO is operationalized as a moderating variable, with controls for firm size, leverage, R&D, age and management turnover. Findings BEI significantly enhances FP, validating contingency theory’s governance–performance linkage. However, GO negatively moderates this relationship, attenuating BEI’s efficiency due to socio-political objectives and bureaucratic constraints. Enterprises with high GO exhibit weaker alignment between governance rigor and FP. Robustness checks using alternative performance metrics (ROA and ROE) and fixed-effects models confirm these results. Research limitations/implications The focus on Chinese listed firms limits generalizability to other emerging markets. Unobserved factors, such as regional policy variations or market competition, may further influence governance dynamics. Future studies should explore cross-country comparisons. Originality/value This research contributes by proposing BEI as a novel composite governance measurement, advancing beyond fragmented analyses of board attributes. Providing empirical evidence from China’s hybrid economy, offering policymakers actionable insights to balance state influence with market-driven governance.
k: board of directors; corporate governance; state ownership; firm financial performance; board size; board independence; CEO duality; board meeting frequency; political connections; board financial expertise; contingency theory; moderating effect; Shanghai Stock Exchange; Chinese listed companies; economic value added; Tobin's Q

t: The consequences of audit firm mobility for attestation services across states
a: This study investigates how audit firm-level spatial licensing requirements affect audit market competition and audit quality, focusing on small (triennially inspected) audit firms, for which licensing frictions are most relevant. Exploiting the staggered state-level adoption of CPA firm mobility provisions that remove spatial licensing barriers, we find that adoption increases competition among small audit firms, as reflected by lower market concentration and greater first-time entry by small out-of-state auditors. Firm mobility adoption also improves audit quality, as indicated by a lower likelihood of client misstatements. These effects are concentrated in less competitive audit markets and among auditors with higher PCAOB deficiency rates. Audit quality improvements extend to both incumbent auditors and new out-of-state entrants, and we find no evidence of audit fee discounting. Overall, our results suggest that removing spatial licensing barriers fosters a more competitive small audit firm market while improving audit outcomes, without increasing audit costs.
k: audit market competition; audit quality; small audit firms; market concentration

t: Teacher–AI Collaboration to Support Assessment and Feedback: A Case Study in Norwegian Secondary Education
a: Recent advancements in Generative AI (GenAI) demonstrate strong potential for enhancing student evaluation and assessment practices through complementary and symmetric human-AI collaboration. This study examines the dispositions, perceived benefits, and challenges that teachers experience when they and GenAI complement one another in providing formative assessment and feedback. Partnering with a leading GenAI-powered EdTech platform, we conducted a case study in a Norwegian secondary school using Learny, a GenAI-supported feedback tool. Qualitative data were collected from teachers who employed Learny in their feedback practices. The findings indicate that teachers were generally curious and open to using GenAI, while emphasizing the need to maintain professional responsibility. They valued GenAI's capacity to save time, offer inspiration, and deliver timely feedback, yet raised concerns about feedback quality, lack of relational and contextual awareness, and the risk of student over-reliance on such feedback. The study contributes to the growing literature on hybrid intelligence in education by identifying conditions under which GenAI can effectively support, rather than replace, human educators. It underscores the centrality of teacher agency in AI-supported feedback and assessment practices and outlines key implications for pedagogy, future GenAI system design, and sustainable implementation.
k: generative AI; teacher-AI collaboration; formative assessment; feedback; hybrid intelligence; teacher agency; secondary education; teacher perceptions; professional responsibility

t: Beyond Tariff Effects: The Impact of Trade Policy Uncertainty on Chinese Exports to the U.S. in the Trade War
a: This paper investigates the impact of trade policy uncertainty (TPU) resulting from the imposition of additional tariffs on Chinese exports to the U.S. during the U.S.‐China Trade War. Using monthly trade data spanning from 2015 to 2019, we find that TPU, measured as the tariff gap, reduces export value and export quantity, and raises export price. TPU roughly accounted for approximately 76.70% of the decline in China's export value to the U.S. during the trade war. Heterogeneity analyses reveal that the effects of TPU on export value are less pronounced for products with relatively low elasticity of substitution, intermediate goods (relative to consumption goods), and products with medium skill and technology intensity. Further mechanism analysis indicates that TPU reduces China's export value to the U.S. through sunk costs, decreasing export market entries and increasing export market exits. Quality competition can partly account for the positive impact of TPU on export price. Our study shows that TPU leads to a welfare loss for U.S. consumers and importers by increasing the unit import price and reducing the variety of imported products.
k: trade policy uncertainty; US-China trade war; tariffs; export value; export prices; export quantity; sunk costs; quality competition; elasticity of substitution; intermediate goods; welfare loss

journal: Journal of Personal Selling & Sales Management
t: Changing the narrative: introducing the CARE framework for salesperson well-being
a: Although there has been a recent increase in research on salesperson well-being, much of it remains fragmented, using abstract frameworks with general rather than individualized implications for practice. In contrast, this research takes an ethics-of-care lens to present a holistic, proactive, and personalized process for sustained salesperson well-being. Adopting a hermeneutic approach, we build on existing sales research, practitioner literature, and in-depth interviews with both sales leaders and frontline salespeople to develop the CARE framework—Cultivate, Assess, Reinforce, Empower—and situate it along a Continuum of Care that spans promotion, prevention, treatment, and recovery. CARE complements established approaches by embedding a continual, relational process of care into everyday sales management, while articulating tensions and tradeoffs. This framework highlights the dual nature of care in sales organizations: the provision of resources and support structures and the cultivation of emotional trust, psychological safety, and a culture of well-being. A key insight is that resources must be paired with genuine sentiment to deliver a positive benefit for frontline salespeople. We conclude with a future research agenda integrating our ethics-of-care framework into existing sales research streams.
k: CARE framework; care ethics; sales management; psychological safety; emotional trust; well-being culture; continuum of care; sales leadership

journal: Journal of the Japanese and International Economies
t: The role of cyclical inflation: Evidence from Japan
a: Monitoring inflation is central to policymaking, yet it is often difficult to separate demand-driven inflation pressure from transitory price movements driven by sector-specific or institutional factors. This paper constructs a cyclically sensitive inflation (CSI) index for Japan by aggregating sectoral inflations with weights reflecting their correlations with business-cycle movements. An analysis of the estimated weights reveals that sectors susceptible to significant deviations from overall inflation, such as those affected by energy pass-through, policy shifts, weather, or rapid quality improvements, generally receive small or zero weights. Consequently, the CSI series remains robust under various alternative weightings. Using monthly data from 1983 to 2022, we find that macro-financial variables contain predictive information for CSI over time. In evidence from exogenous structural shocks using externally identified oil-market disturbances, CSI is less responsive on impact to transitory cost-push movements but reacts more strongly and persistently to demand-driven changes. Forecast comparisons indicate that CSI improves predictions for the headline CPI relative to traditional headline and core measures, although adding a standard slack indicator yields only limited and inconsistent improvements once CSI is included. Finally, the inflation decomposition analysis indicates that medium- and long-term inflation persistence is primarily associated with the cyclical component captured by CSI, rather than with residual acyclical fluctuations. Overall, CSI complements headline and core inflation measures by providing a timely measure of cyclical inflation pressures and aiding the understanding of persistent inflation dynamics.
k: sectoral inflation; cost-push inflation; inflation persistence; oil market shocks; inflation forecasting; core inflation; inflation decomposition; Japan

t: Cost-utility analysis of Edaravone compared to Riluzole in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) in Iran
a: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a devastating disease that damages motor neurons. Currently, two drugs, Riluzole and Edaravone, have been shown to slow the progression of this condition. This study aimed to evaluate the cost-utility of Edaravone compared to Riluzole in ALS patients. This is an economic evaluation and cost-utility analysis from Iran’s health system perspective using a 10-year and 20-year Markov model. Cost data were collected from medical records and expert interviews, while clinical outcomes and transition probabilities were obtained from a clinical trial study. The robustness of the findings was tested through both deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analysis. Data was analyzed using Excel 2019 and TreeAge Pro 2020 software. The findings of this study indicated that the cost of treatment and QALYs obtained from Edaravone (58,077 PPP$ and 1.66) compared to Riluzole (53,216 PPP$ and 1.37) were estimated to be higher in Iran. The calculated ICUR was equal to 16,704 PPP$ which is considered to be a cost-effective option in terms of the cost-effectiveness threshold to treat the patients with ALS. Furthermore, a one-way sensitivity analysis showed that the model is most affected by the cost discount rate and the price of Edaravone. Edaravone was identified as the best treatment strategy in 66% of simulations, making it the preferred option across different willingness to pay scenarios. The findings of the study indicated that the Edaravone may be a more cost-effective and affordable option compared to the Riluzole. Consequently, the availability of this drug in the country is likely to improve the quality of life and increase the survival rates of patients.
k: amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; edaravone; riluzole; cost-utility analysis; cost-effectiveness; Markov model; quality-adjusted life years; Iran health system; drug pricing; treatment costs

t: From decision patience to process patience: A decision–process integration of the choice to wait and the experience of waiting
a: Consumer impatience has long been examined through the lens of intertemporal choice, where patience is inferred from decisions to accept delayed rewards. Yet, this conceptualization captures only the choice to wait, not the experience of waiting. Sweeny's Process Model of Patience (PMP) shifts the focus from temporal preferences to temporal affect, defining impatience as a negatively valenced emotional response to objectionable delays and patience as the active regulation of this emotion. In this commentary, I bridge these two traditions by mapping the psychological drivers of intertemporal choice—affective urges, cognitive representations, construal, subjective time perception, and future‐self connectedness—onto the mechanisms that shape waiting experiences. This decision–process integration of impatience reveals where the two perspectives converge, where they diverge, and why these distinctions matter for understanding consumer behavior. I propose several testable predictions illustrating how choice patience and process patience dissociate, how motivations and mental representations shift across the decision–waiting timeline, and how environmental cues can reduce uncertainty at choice yet heighten impatience during the wait. Together, these insights suggest a more complete temporal model of impatience—one that begins before the decision is made and continues throughout the delay that follows.
k: consumer impatience; patience; intertemporal choice; waiting experience; construal; subjective time perception; environmental cues

t: Non-Bank Financial Intermediation as an Alternative to Traditional Banking for New Business Creation
a: Growing financial innovation has led to the expansion of non-bank financial intermediation (NBFI) as a key ingredient for new entrepreneurs dealing with limited access to traditional finance. In this study, we seek to identify the effect of NBFI’s development on new business creation, in contrast to that of traditional banking. To this end, we examine a panel of 21 European countries over the period 2006–2021 using two-way fixed-effects panel regression models and annual data drawn from several publicly available databases. We employ two alternative measures of entrepreneurship: total early-stage entrepreneurship, which includes both formal and informal entrepreneurship, and new business registration, which captures formal businesses only. The results indicate that the development of NBFI matters more for informal entrepreneurship, while traditional banking is more relevant to businesses operating in the formal sector. This finding is particularly evident in the period after 2017, which coincides with the consolidation of Basel III standards in Europe. Informal entrepreneurs may rely primarily on informal sources of finance in the early stages of business creation and turn to traditional banks only later, as their businesses become formalised. Moreover, new business creation occurs mainly when the two financial intermediaries act more as complements rather than substitutes.
k: shadow banking; conventional banks; startups; entrepreneurship; informal entrepreneurship; formal sector; access to finance; Basel III; financial innovation; informal finance

t: How to Talk with the Academic Community about Contested Knowledge: A Confrontational-Reflexive Interview Model
a: Interviewing academics about contested knowledge presents significant methodological challenges, as the interview situation often activates “official” professional repertoires that conceal ambivalence and the active construction of epistemic boundaries. To address these limitations, the authors propose and evaluate the confrontational-reflexive interview model (CRIM), a research design aimed at systematically eliciting reflexivity and analyzing boundary-work in situ . The model treats the interview not as a neutral information extraction tool but as a structured sequence of meaning-making occasions. Stage 1 establishes a baseline narrative in expert interviews and focus groups, which is subsequently disrupted by a standardized “confrontation stimulus”—a scholarly text explicitly challenging the dominant disciplinary consensus—forcing participants to negotiate their position against a credible internal critique. Stage 2, conducted approximately one month later via asynchronous written correspondence, introduces temporal distance to test the stability and revisability of these accounts outside the immediate pressure of the face-to-face interaction. Drawing on a study of political scientists’ discourse on conspiracy theories, the authors demonstrate that although standard interviewer probes often fail to unsettle “official” narratives, the combination of a third-party textual confrontation and delayed reflection successfully reveals the specific conditions under which experts reproduce, repair, or redraw the boundaries of legitimate knowledge. The authors argue that CRIM contributes to sociological methodology by offering a replicable framework for observing expertise as a contingent, interactional performance.
k: contested knowledge; reflexivity; limits of knowledge; boundary work; expert interviews; disciplinary consensus; conspiracy theories; political scientists; legitimacy of knowledge

t: Implications of the European union carbon border adjustment mechanism for the downstream aluminium industry in India
a: This study examines the potential implications of the European Union (EU) Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) for the downstream aluminium sector in India. Using average emissions intensity values in India and the EU, the study quantifies the potential CBAM costs for Indian aluminium exporters and examines how changes in emissions intensity or domestic carbon pricing could affect these liabilities. Downstream aluminium firms are likely to incur a substantial amount of tariffs because of CBAM, posing a significant challenge to export competitiveness. The paper recommends supportive measures for competitiveness and sustainability in India’s aluminium sector under changing global scenario.
k: CBAM; emission intensity; carbon pricing; export competitiveness; tariffs

t: Sweetening the Empire: Sugar and Western-Style Confectionery in Modern Japan and Taiwan
a: This dissertation examines how Western-style confectionery such as caramel, chocolate, chewing gum, and other sweets became intertwined with Japan’s empire-building from the Meiji period (1868–1912) to the early postwar years. While there have been extensive studies on sugar labor, empire, and capitalism, this dissertation focuses on what happened after the sugar was harvested until it was manufactured into delicious confectionery goods. Using a wide array of sources from colonial and corporate archives, science magazines, trade journals, films, artworks, oral history, and diaries, I examine three major confectionery companies—Morinaga, Meiji, and Niitaka—and how the production and marketing of their commodities were entangled with Japan’s imperial expansion. The production process reveals the unexamined colonial networks through which these companies sourced raw materials like sugar, cocoa, and banana powder from Japan’s tropical colony, Taiwan. When these products were sold across the empire, they were marketed alongside messages that embodied Japan’s imperial ambitions and colonial ideology. During the total war (1937–1945), sugar and confectionery continued to play a significant role by sustaining soldiers’ stamina on the battlefield and enticing enemy children to develop affection toward Japan. Altogether, this dissertation argues that Western-style confectionery should be understood as a commodity of the Japanese Empire: its production expanded alongside the empire, while its sweetness, in turn, helped sustain imperial power by functioning as a form of “soft power.”
k: sugar; Japanese Empire; Meiji period; Japanese colonial Taiwan; chocolate; caramel; chewing gum; colonial networks; colonial ideology; soft power; total war; wartime food supply; Theobroma cacao; banana powder; food marketing

t: External monitoring or noise interference? Negative media tone, audit quality and cost of debt financing
a: Purpose This study examines the impact of key audit quality dimensions on the cost of debt financing and investigates whether negative media tone moderates this relationship. It aims to reveal whether negative media tone functions as an external monitoring or as informational noise in debt pricing. Design/methodology/approach Using a sample of A-share listed firms in China from 2014 to 2023, this study employs fixed effects models to examine the impact of audit quality dimensions and their interaction with negative media tone on cost of debt financing. Findings The findings show that larger auditor size and dual-level industry specialization significantly reduce cost of debt, while higher audit fees and modified audit opinions increase it. These effects are more pronounced for firms audited by domestic leading audit firms than those audited by the Big Four. Negative media tone acts as a monitoring amplifier, reinforcing the market's pricing response to audit quality signals rather than distorting it. This moderating effect remains consistent across both state-owned and non-state-owned firms. Originality/value This study extends signaling theory and media governance literature by documenting how negative media tone reinforces the pricing effect of audit quality in debt markets. It provides new evidence from an emerging market where formal and informal oversight mechanisms jointly influence capital market perceptions, with practical implications for improving credit risk assessment.
k: audit quality; cost of debt; external monitoring; informational noise; debt pricing; audit firm size; audit fees; modified audit opinions; Big 4 auditors; state-owned enterprises; credit risk assessment; signaling theory; media governance; Chinese listed companies

journal: Canadian Journal of Agricultural Economics / Revue Canadienne d Agroeconomie
t: Environmentally adjusted productivity growth and shadow prices for dairy farms
a: We estimate the environmentally adjusted productivity growth and shadow price for Ontario dairy farms. We use an input‐oriented directional distance function and farm‐level data from 2000 to 2020. First, we find that while GHG emissions per cow increase with higher milk yields, emission intensity decreases as milk yield per cow increases. We also find that emission intensity decreased over the study period. Second, we find that environmentally adjusted productivity growth is higher than unadjusted productivity growth. Technological change contributed more to both environmentally adjusted and unadjusted productivity growth than did efficiency change. Third, the estimated shadow price for GHG emissions was CAN$286 per metric ton.
k: dairy farms; emission intensity; milk yield; technological change; efficiency change; directional distance function

t: Impact of Retail Investor Attention on Option Returns: A Nonparametric Test Approach
a: The surge in retail investor participation in the options market, driven by innovations such as zero-commission trading, raises questions about how investor behavior influences market outcomes. We examine the relationship between retail investor attention and option returns using a nonparametric test tailored to nonstationary time series. Unlike traditional Granger causality methods, our approach accommodates nonlinear, nonstationary dynamics by combining advances in conditional independence testing with time-varying kernel density estimation. Our results show that investor attention is closely linked to option returns, particularly their second moment, suggesting that options favored by retail investors are riskier and more volatile.
k: retail investor attention; option returns; retail investor participation; non-stationary time series; conditional independence testing; option volatility; investor behavior

journal: International Journal of Pharmaceutical and Healthcare Marketing
t: Exploring consumer responses to short-form video marketing in the medical aesthetics sector
a: Purpose This study aims to investigate the influence of short-form videos on consumers’ purchase intentions toward medical aesthetic products, focusing on how informational value, interactivity, credibility and visual appeal affect perceived value. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected through an online survey and analyzed using structural equation modeling to examine the relationships among content attributes, perceived value and purchase intention. Findings Credibility, informational value, visual appeal and interactivity significantly affect perceived value, which in turn influences purchase intention. Credibility emerged as the most influential attribute, highlighting the importance of trust and expertise in high-involvement, high-risk contexts. Originality/value This study extends digital marketing research to the medical aesthetics industry, demonstrating how multiple content attributes jointly shape consumer perceptions and purchase intentions. Practical insights are provided for marketers to design effective, credible and engaging short-form video content.
k: short-form video marketing; aesthetic medicine; purchase intention; perceived value; credibility; value of information; interactivity; visual appeal; consumer trust; high-involvement products

journal: International Journal of Learning and Change
t: Work-from-home stressors and work-life conflict among working women: a sequential mediation of role overload and emotional exhaustion
a: This research paper will explore the effects of work-from-home stressors (WFS) on work-life conflict (WLF) among employed women in the Indian IT industry, and the mediating effects of role overload (RO) and emotional exhaustion (EE). To achieve a cross-sectional research design, primary data were collected from 433 respondents using a structured questionnaire comprising 30 items based on existing scales. The results show that WFS has a considerable positive effect on RO, EE, and WLF. Moreover, RO has a strong impact on EE and WLF, and EE has a great positive impact on WLF. Mediation analysis proves the mediation of RO and EE in the relations between WFS and WLF separately and in series. The research emphasises the importance of structural and psychological processes in the development of work-life conflict and offers implications for the management of the remote work problem among working women.
k: work-life conflict; women's employment; role overload; emotional exhaustion; remote work; Indian IT industry; mediation; occupational stress

journal: International Journal of Logistics Systems and Management
t: Depot location for a multi-depot transport problem with electric vehicles
a: The world regulations related to the emission of greenhouse gases (GHG) have contributed to the evolution of the green vehicle market, thus making great strides in sales and technology. The electric vehicle, which has a limited range, is one of the best alternatives to the conventional combustion vehicle. In this paper, we consider a multi-depot electric capacitated vehicle routing problem (MDECVRP) where the objective is to find the optimal routing strategy with the minimum total energy consumption as well as the minimum total cost of opening depots, while respecting the constraints related to the problem. For that, a mathematical model and a resolution approach based on a large neighbourhood search are proposed to solve the studied problem. Finally, numerical results related to three classes of the MDECVRP are given to validate the aforementioned approach by making a comparison with the results obtained by the CPLEX solver for small instances.
k: electric vehicles; depot location; energy optimization; large neighborhood search; green logistics; greenhouse gas emissions; vehicle routing optimization

t: The Limits of Weakened Stare Decisis: Cautionary Lessons from the United States for Australia
a: Both the High Court of Australia and the United States Supreme Court have recently revisited the doctrine of stare decisis and its role in constitutional settings. This article examines how and when apex courts are willing to overturn their prior decisions on questions of constitutional interpretation, and whether a weakened application of stare decisis is appropriate in this context. Drawing on comparative representation-reinforcing theory, and applying it to contemporary United States constitutional experience, we identify cautionary insights for Australian constitutionalism. We argue that while a measured weakening of stare decisis in the constitutional context may be justified, such weakening goes too far when it is or is perceived to be the cause or side-effect of the politicisation of judicial decision-making.
k: judicial precedent; constitutional interpretation; High Court of Australia; United States Supreme Court; constitutional law; comparative constitutional law

journal: Journal of Purchasing and Supply Management
t: Building resilience amidst a crisis: An automaker’s procurement journey to secure semiconductor supply
a: With procurement as the core function for managing supply, this study investigates how procurement contributes to building supply chain resilience during high-impact and long-lasting disruptions. Drawing on the adaptive cycle perspective of resilience, we investigate how procurement influences potential and connectedness in procurement and supply management (PSM) to support persistence, adaptation, and transformation in response to long-lasting, high-impact disruptions. Using in-depth data from a case of a commercial vehicle original equipment manufacturer, our findings show that procurement not only enables operational continuity through internal coordination and external information flows, but also facilitates strategic adaptation by reconfiguring processes and relationships. Notably, procurement drives the transformation of a firm’s PSM by institutionalizing new roles internally and redefining its role in the supply network. We propose a conceptual framework that links procurement to changes in potential and connectedness and theorizes how procurement contributes to resilience, based on an adaptive view of resilience.
k: supply chain resilience; procurement; semiconductor supply; supply chain disruption; strategic adaptation; information flow; operational continuity

t: Estimating endogenous ordinal treatment effects with high‐dimensional instruments and covariates
a: We propose a novel two‐stage approach to estimate the causal effect of an endogenous ordinal treatment variable on an outcome, using high‐dimensional instruments and covariates. In the first stage, we apply a penalized proportional odds reduced‐form model to estimate the ordinal treatment propensity score and optimal instrument. In the second stage, we substitute ordinal data with predicted values and derive the ordinal logistic instrumental variable estimator (OLIVE) for the endogenous causal effect via least squares regression. Our model allows the number of covariates to exceed the sample size; in such scenarios, we use double selection to identify key controls and introduce the double selection plus ordinal logistic instrumental variable estimator (DS‐OLIVE). We prove DS‐OLIVE is root‐n consistent and asymptotically normal. Simulations demonstrate that OLIVE and DS‐OLIVE surpass existing methods in bias and mean squared error. Finally, we apply our method to a case study assessing parental health's impact on children's study performance.
k: high-dimensional covariates; double selection; root-n consistency; asymptotic normality; parental health; children's academic achievement

t: Controlling Shareholder's Share Pledging and the Corporate Artificial Intelligence Washing: Evidence From China
a: Controlling shareholder share pledging exposes the controlling shareholder to the risk of losing corporate control in the event of a stock price decline. This paper aims to examine whether controlling shareholder share pledging drives corporate AI washing, and to identify the mechanisms through which this effect operates. This study indicates that controlling shareholder share pledging exerts a significant and robust exacerbating effect on corporate AI washing. The mechanism through which this effect operates lies in heightened earnings aggressiveness and aggravated information opacity. Besides, agency problems significantly strengthen this positive relationship, as controlling shareholders with greater agency discretion face fewer internal constraints on opportunistic AI disclosures. Analyst coverage, however, attenuates this exacerbating effect, consistent with the view that external monitoring by information intermediaries disciplines controlling shareholders' opportunistic behavior and mitigates the informational consequences of share pledging. From the perspective of controlling shareholders' financing behavior, this paper examines the driving effect of share pledging on corporate AI washing through heightened earnings aggressiveness and aggravated information opacity, thereby introducing this emerging opportunistic practice into the literature on the real effects of share pledging. Meanwhile, agency problems reinforce this effect from the internal governance perspective, while analyst coverage attenuates it from the external monitoring perspective, providing practical insights for regulators and investors to curb AI washing through the integration of internal and external governance mechanisms.
k: AI disclosure; information opacity; principal-agent problem; analyst coverage; corporate governance; Chinese listed companies

journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Health Management
t: Global Trend for Human Resource Development Mapping for Pharmacists
a: Pharmacist workforce planning remains a global challenge, with fragmented evidence and no comprehensive framework across diverse contexts. This paper aims to analyze structures and patterns of knowledge on pharmacist workforce planning and management at the discipline level. This study employed a systematic bibliometric analysis of 364 Scopus-indexed articles published between 1968 and 2024. The analysis was done using citation analysis, co-occurrence network analysis, and bibliographic coupling to identify key themes, patterns of connections, and directions of knowledge development. The results indicate that studies on pharmacist workforce planning can be clustered to reflect key dimensions of the workforce system, including strategic workforce management, specialty distribution, supply-demand analysis, and work system and technology design. Existing literature remains constrained by static frameworks and insufficient integration of roles, competencies, technology, and system dynamics. This study structures global knowledge and identifies future research directions to support forward looking pharmacist workforce planning in complex systems.
k: human resource development; specialty distribution; supply and demand analysis; work system design; research trends

t: To sign or not to sign initiatives to reform research evaluation: A discussion of the pros and cons
a: The integration of bibliometrics into science governance has fundamentally transformed scientific practices, leading to unintended consequences such as goal displacement and citizen bibliometrics. In response, international reform movements like the Agreement on Reforming Research Assessment (CoARA) advocate for responsible research assessment and the primacy of qualitative peer review. This short communication examines the commonalities and differences of these movements and weighs the pros and cons for research organizations considering signing them. While endorsement offers socio-political legitimacy and can catalyze internal modernization toward improved evaluation processes, organizations are also confronted with certain challenges. These include the potential neglect of disciplinary evaluation cultures, the high administrative burden of qualitative review, and the prevalent risk of purely symbolic uptake. Acknowledging the limitations of current empirical evidence, this commentary concludes that the future of research assessment relies not on universal declarations, but on the development of process-specific evaluation designs. Strategic principles for implementation – such as tailoring assessments to specific occasions, respecting epistemic diversity, safeguarding data sovereignty, empowering evaluation committees, evaluating assessment procedures, and professionalizing evaluative bibliometrics – are proposed to advance responsible evaluative practices.
k: research assessment reform; CoARA; responsible research assessment; goal displacement; evaluation committee; data sovereignty; epistemic diversity; research organization

t: Hydraulic Barrier Optimization Using Random‐Walk Particle Tracking in Heterogeneous Media: Effects of Dispersion, Particle Discretization and Algorithmic Initialization
a: Hydraulic barriers (HBs) are commonly used for solute plume containment in polluted aquifers. Their long‐term sustainability depends on minimizing the cumulative pumping rate, , required to ensure plume capture. Lagrangian random‐walk particle tracking (RWPT) is an effective approach for simulating advective‐dispersive transport to wells. However, as this method typically requires a large number of particles, , RWPT‐based simulation–optimization (SO) can be computationally demanding. This work presents an SO framework that couples a warm‐start genetic algorithm with parallel RWPT to identify minimal pumping rates for HB containment in a computationally efficient manner. The framework was applied in a Monte Carlo study using stochastic hydraulic conductivity fields, with ranging from to . Results showed that optimal values were jointly conditioned by transport processes, particle discretization, and algorithmic initialization. Under advection‐only transport, was nearly insensitive to . In contrast, when local dispersion was included, and its variability increased with . The influence of particle discretization depended strongly on the adopted recovery criterion, becoming substantially weaker when incomplete particle recovery was allowed. Neglecting local dispersion can therefore underestimate pumping requirements, particularly under stringent recovery criteria and increasing particle resolution. Warm‐start initialization generally identified lower solutions than cold initialization while also reducing computational time. These findings demonstrate that particle discretization, local dispersion and the recovery criterion should be considered explicitly when optimizing HBs, and that warm‐start strategies can substantially improve computational efficiency in RWPT‐based SO workflows.
k: hydraulic barriers; random walk particle tracking; simulation-based optimization; genetic algorithm; warm-start initialization; local dispersion; aquifer heterogeneity; groundwater contamination

t: The numerical detective: EDA as methodology for managerial insight
a: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), originally framed by John Tukey as a discipline of visual reasoning and judgement, is increasingly vital to managerial decision-making in environments characterized by high-dimensional and irregular data. This paper reframes EDA as a contemporary analytical methodology that enhances managerial insight. We do this by combining modern transformation techniques with visual diagnostics to reveal structure, surface anomalies and challenge assumptions. Drawing on case studies in environmental science, digital forensics and public policy, we show how EDA enables managers to act as numerical detectives—interrogating uncertainty, validating assumptions and identifying operational risks earlier in the decision cycle. Across these cases, EDA exposes concealed variability and distributional irregularities that conventional reporting pipelines overlook. We conclude by discussing implications for analytical reproducibility, auditability and the expanding role of EDA in organizational diagnostics and risk-informed strategic decision-making.
k: exploratory data analysis; management decision-making; visual diagnostics; high-dimensional data; transformation techniques; uncertainty; operational risk; analytical reproducibility; auditability; organizational diagnosis; risk-based decision making; digital forensics; public policy

t: Estimating the natural real interest rate in Lithuania: a semi-structural approach
a: This paper estimates the natural real interest rate (r∗) for Lithuania over the period 2000–2025 and assesses the implied monetary policy conditions. The paper employs a semi-structural unobserved-components model tailored to a small, open, and converging economy by incorporating real effective exchange rate dynamics, while also enhancing output-gap identification and exploring the role of survey-based inflation expectations. The results indicate that Lithuania's r∗ was relatively high in the early 2000s, declined markedly during the global financial crisis, remained persistently low thereafter, and returned to positive values in recent years. Following the euro's adoption, Lithuania's estimated r∗ exhibits closer co-movement with the euro area's natural rate, consistent with deeper economic and financial integration. Estimates of the real interest rate gap suggest that monetary conditions have been predominantly accommodative historically and broadly neutral in recent periods.
k: real effective exchange rate; inflation expectations; 2008 financial crisis; euro adoption; Lithuania; small open economy

journal: International Journal of Shipping and Transport Logistics
t: Global trade dynamics of the shipbreaking industry: a complex network analysis approach
a: This study investigates the structural characteristics of the global shipbreaking trade network using complex network analysis and bilateral trade data for 2014, 2017, 2020, and 2023. The analysis identifies Bangladesh, India, Turkey, and Pakistan as central nodes in the network, reflecting their role as major destinations for end-of-life vessels. Indicators such as indegree, outdegree, PageRank, authority, and modularity were employed to examine connectivity patterns, community structures, and network vulnerability. The results reveal a declining number of nodes and edges, indicating growing concentration of shipbreaking activities in a limited set of countries. Modularity analysis shows the emergence of regional clusters, particularly linking South Asian and Mediterranean hubs, while vulnerability tests confirm that the removal of highly central countries significantly weakens the network. These findings suggest that although shipbreaking supports resource recovery and cost efficiency, its concentration heightens risks related to sustainability, safety, and resilience. Overall, the study adds to the limited literature on shipbreaking and suggests that geographically diversifying ship recycling under harmonised environmental and labour standards could mitigate risks and support long-term sustainability.
k: shipbreaking; ship recycling; international trade networks; complex networks; network centrality; network modularity; network vulnerability; regional clusters; Bangladesh; India; Turkey; Pakistan; South Asia; Mediterranean; sustainability risk

journal: International Journal for Quality in Health Care
t: Targeting what matters: a quasi-experimental controlled before-and-after study on targeted double checks in parenteral medication administration
a: BACKGROUND: Parenteral medication administration is associated with a substantial risk of medication errors. Independent double-checking by two nurses is widely mandated to reduce this risk; however, evidence is lacking, compliance is inconsistent, and the procedure is time-consuming. Medication safety organizations increasingly recommend targeted double-checking of high-risk medications, yet the impact of such a strategy in clinical practice remains unclear. This study evaluated the effect of implementing targeted double-checking, alongside barcode verification, on compliance with predefined safe administration procedures during parenteral medication administration. METHODS: A quasi-experimental controlled before-and-after study was conducted on two comparable surgical wards in a Dutch university hospital between June 2022 and January 2024. On the intervention ward, parenteral administrations were categorized as high- or low-risk, with double-checking required only for high-risk administrations alongside mandatory barcode verification. The control ward continued universal double-checking combined with barcode verification for both high- and low-risk administrations. The primary outcome was the percentage of safe administrations, defined as compliance with predefined safety administration procedures according to administration risk level. Secondary outcomes included barcode verification rates, double-check application rates, medication errors, voluntarily reported incidents, and administration time as a measure of efficiency. Outcomes were assessed using disguised observations and retrospective data analysis. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and chi-square or Fisher's exact tests. RESULTS: A total of 250 administrations were observed. Compliance with safe administrations increased on the intervention ward from 0% to 41% (P < .001) and on the control ward from 16% to 35% (P = .025). Double-check application decreased on the intervention ward (60%-11%, P < .001) but increased on the control ward (0%-16%, P = .002). Barcode verification during observations increased on the intervention ward (53%-76%, P = .007) and decreased on the control ward (71%-31%, P < .001). Retrospective analysis showed improved patient and medication barcode verification on the intervention ward (15% (1446/9567) to 51% (579/1133), P < .001) and a decline on the control ward (18% (1759/9857) to 12% (150/1229), P < .001). Implementation of targeted double-checking was associated with an estimated saving of 48 minutes of nursing time per day. No medication errors or incidents were reported. CONCLUSION: Targeted double-checking combined with barcode verification appears to improve compliance with safe administration procedures during parenteral medication administration; however, improvements on the control ward preclude definitive conclusions regarding effectiveness. This targeted strategy may provide a sustainable alternative by reducing unnecessary procedural b
k: medication errors; high-risk medications; drug safety; nurse compliance; surgical wards; timing of drug administration; patient safety interventions; implementation evaluation; patient safety culture; nursing workload; hospital ward management

journal: Journal of Competition Law and Economics
t: Calibrating Generalized Nested Logit Demand
a: The commonly used nested logit (NL) demand system allows for some flexibility in substitution patterns, but each good in the market must be assigned to exactly one nest. The generalized nested logit (GNL) is a more flexible demand system that allows for overlapping nests and reflects a richness in substitution patterns that can be important for many contexts. This paper considers what information is required to calibrate the parameters of a GNL demand system with products belonging to two nests, and shows through empirical examples how the parameters can be calibrated using data that is typically available to competition regulators during an investigation.
k: demand systems; parameter calibration; substitution patterns; market power; competition law; antitrust investigation

t: Optimal Piecewise Linear Approximations for Sigmoid, Tanh, Probability Density and Cumulative Distribution Functions: Tabular Form and R Package pwlapprox2d
a: We present information in tabular form about optimal piecewise linear (PWL) approximations of the sigmoid and tanh activation functions as used in neural networks, as well as the probability density and cumulative distribution functions of the Normal and log-Normal distributions. The presented approximations minimise the maximum absolute difference between the PWL function and the continuous function being modelled; we also provide information on optimal over- and underestimators. We provide information on the optimal breakpoint locations for different numbers of breakpoints in a series of tables, as well as the accuracy provided by these approximations. This allows practitioners to utilise the PWL approximations whenever needed; for example, to enable the use of mixed-integer linear programming techniques to solve problems where these functions may appear, or to approximate integrals. The provided optimal breakpoint locations lead to an improvement over a uniform breakpoint location of the maximum absolute difference of up to 95% and an average of 84% among the six functions. This information is available online at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16362215 and can be recreated using the R package pwlapprox2d [1].
k: piecewise linear approximation; sigmoid function; tanh function; activation functions; normal distribution; lognormal distribution; cumulative distribution function; probability density function; breakpoint location; mixed-integer linear programming; integral approximation

t: Living with the river: Territorial imaginaries, risk cultures, and everyday adaptation in a flood-prone neighborhood
a: As climate change intensifies the frequency and severity of floods, questions about the habitability of flood-prone territories are gaining urgency. This paper explores how residents of a floodplain neighborhood in Lachute, Québec (Canada), perceive, inhabit, and adapt to recurring floods. Based on 29 semi-structured interviews and qualitative fieldwork conducted in 2023, the study analyzes how lived experience, emotional ties, and symbolic representations shape risk imaginaries and adaptive behavior. Findings reveal two coexisting geographical imaginaries: one rooted in long-term exposure and a logic of cohabitation with the river; the other shaped by distance, denial, or defense. These imaginaries generate divergent attitudes toward adaptation, preparedness, and public policy. The paper introduces a conceptual framework linking representations of the river, flood events, and risk, highlighting the cultural dimensions of flood resilience. In doing so, it challenges dominant regulatory approaches based on static zoning and hydraulic models, and calls for more context-sensitive, territorialized forms of governance. The study contributes to debates on risk governance by foregrounding the symbolic and material dimensions of living with water.
k: flood adaptation; risk culture; flood resilience; risk governance; territorial imaginaries; climate change and flooding; flood preparedness; river symbolism

t: When caring depletes: the paradox of leading employee wellbeing during a prolonged crisis – evidence from the Australian resources sector
a: Purpose The protracted COVID-19 crisis placed substantial demands on managers in the Australian resources industry. While workers' wellbeing received increased attention during this period, much less is known about how managers sustained their own wellbeing while providing care, reassurance, and operational continuity. Drawing on the JD–R model, paradox theory, and moral strain perspectives, we examine wellbeing-oriented leadership during a sustained crisis. We focus on how leadership behaviour operated as both a resource for employees and a demand on managers, shaping their own wellbeing experiences and leadership identity. Design/methodology/approach An interpretative phenomenological approach (IPA) was employed. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 32 managers in the Australian mining, oil, and gas sector. The interview accounts were analysed using IPA to examine how participants made sense of responsibility, care, and uncertainty during a prolonged crisis. Findings The findings indicate that leadership during a prolonged crisis embodied a Demand–Resource Paradox (DRP). Practices such as emotional support, constant availability, and responsibility for safety and wellbeing decisions acted as resources for employees while imposing demands on managers. Sustained over time, these practices contributed to the accumulation of psychological strain and resource depletion. Originality/value First, we extend JD–R theory by identifying a Demand–Resource Paradox in which wellbeing-oriented leadership supports workers while depleting managers. Second, we advance moral strain research by showing how moral strain accumulates through prolonged crisis-related responsibility. Third, we reconceptualise crisis leadership as an endurance-based process, distinct from resilience models, by emphasising chronic demands, cumulative depletion, identity reshaping, and the absence of clear recovery periods.
k: COVID-19 pandemic; psychological strain; resource depletion; leadership identity; crisis leadership; job demands-resources model; paradox theory; employee well-being; emotional support

t: Annealed leap-point sampler for multimodal target distributions
a: In Bayesian statistics, exploring high-dimensional multimodal posterior distributions poses major challenges for existing MCMC approaches. This paper introduces the annealed leap-point sampler (ALPS), which augments the target distribution state space with modified annealed (cooled) distributions, in contrast to traditional tempering approaches. The coldest state is chosen such that its annealed density is well-approximated locally by a Laplace approximation. This allows for automated setup of a scalable mode-leaping independence sampler. ALPS requires an exploration component to search for the mode locations, which can either be run adaptively in parallel to improve these mode-jumping proposals, or else as a pre-computation step. A theoretical analysis shows that for a d-dimensional problem the coolest temperature level required only needs to be linear in dimension, $$\mathcal {O}\left( d\right) $$ O d , implying that the number of iterations needed for ALPS to converge is $$\mathcal {O}\left( d\right) $$ O d (typically leading to overall complexity $$\mathcal {O}\left( d^3\right) $$ O d 3 when computational cost per iteration is taken into account). ALPS is illustrated on several complex, multimodal distributions that arise from real-world applications. This includes a seemingly-unrelated regression (SUR) model of longitudinal data from U.S. manufacturing firms, as well as a spectral density model that is used in analytical chemistry for identification of molecular biomarkers.
k: multimodal posterior distributions; mode jumping; tempered distributions; Laplace approximation; high-dimensional Bayesian inference; seemingly unrelated regression; biomarker discovery

t: Measuring Business-Process Distance with Large Language Models
a: Traditional measures of cultural and contextual distance between countries typically rely on arithmetic or geometric comparisons based on survey-based cultural values or country-level statistics. While useful for explaining cross-national variations in behavior, organizational practices, and trade, these measures often lack the granularity and real-world applicability required by international business practitioners. This article takes an exploratory approach, investigating whether the knowledge embedded in large language models can be used to assess differences in industry-specific business processes across countries. Rather than relying on aggregated national indices, the study examines how large language models might reveal nuanced, domain-specific patterns in business practices. The goal of this proof of concept is not to replace existing distance measures, but to explore a complementary, AI-driven perspective that could yield more flexible, detailed, and actionable insights for managing cross-border operations.
k: cultural distance; large language models; cross-border operations

journal: International Journal of Technological Learning, Innovation and Development
t: Research and Development (R&D), Innovation, and Total Factor Productivity: Institutional Enablers in a Longitudinal Study of Ethiopian Enterprises
a: This study examines how research and development (R&D) engagement affects innovation and productivity in Ethiopian businesses, using panel data from 744 firms and a generalised structural equation modelling (GSEM) approach. Results indicate that R&D investment significantly enhances both product and process innovation. However, process innovation has a short-term negative effect on productivity, especially among non-exporting and larger firms. Notably, 71% of firms that do not participate in formal R&D still report product innovation, highlighting the importance of informal knowledge and alternative innovation pathways. Institutional factors play a crucial role in shaping innovation results. Firms with government contracts, access to credit, and those offering workforce training are more likely to innovate. Export orientation and location in the capital city are also linked to a higher likelihood of innovation. Conversely, older and larger firms tend to show lower productivity gains, reflecting structural challenges in adapting to innovation. Overall, the findings reveal that innovation in resource-limited settings is driven not only by R&D expenditure but also by institutional support and firm capabilities. Policies that encourage R&D incentives, training, access to finance, and stronger public-private partnerships are vital to enhancing productivity and fostering inclusive innovation in developing economies.
k: research and development; innovation; total factor productivity; product innovation; process innovation; institutional factors; informal knowledge; public procurement; access to credit; employee training; export orientation; firm size; firm age; public-private partnerships; R&D incentives; developing countries

t: Preparing the Next Generation: How Trust, Gender, and Academic Performance Shape Financial Planning Students' AI Adoption
a: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly incorporated into financial planning education, raising important questions about how future professionals will engage with these tools. This exploratory quantitative study applies Human‐Automation Interaction (HAI) theory to examine how undergraduate financial planning students' trust in ChatGPT, demographic characteristics, and academic performance relate to patterns of AI usage and reliance in the educational context. Non‐parametric tests were used to analyze a primary data set of 60 undergraduate students enrolled in financial planning courses. Results indicate that trust in ChatGPT positively correlates with increased usage frequency and greater reliance on AI for financial advice. Female students report significantly higher usage of ChatGPT than male students, while a lower GPA is associated with a greater reliance on AI for financial advice. These findings offer insights into workforce development in financial planning education, highlighting the importance of trust calibration, gender‐responsive training, and thoughtful AI integration.
k: artificial intelligence adoption; ChatGPT; financial planning education; trust in AI; gender differences; academic performance; GPA; AI reliance; human-automation interaction; financial advice; undergraduate students; workforce development

t: “Thank you for your suggestion”: investigating the relationship between video game influencers’ credibility and gamers’ microtransaction intentions
a: Purpose Influencer marketing has been an interesting development in the video game domain. The focus of the game-based marketing is shifting from advergames to livestream and influencer marketing. Influencer credibility is a critical phenomenon in influencer marketing. Drawing from source credibility theory, this study investigates the effect of influencers’ credibility on microtransaction intentions and explores the mediating role of gamers’ trust in influencers’ suggestions. Additionally, it examines the moderating effect of gamers’ attachment to gaming.Design/Methodology/Approach Data were collected from 225 gamers, and structural equation modeling was used for data analysis.Findings Results revealed a positive relationship between influencer credibility and microtransaction intention and a significant moderating effect of attachment on this relationship.Practical implications Practical implications are suggested for leveraging influencer marketing effectively in the gaming domain. It includes collaboration between the game publisher and the influencers, promotion of in-game items, and persuading gamers towards microtransactions.Research contribution This study empirically validates source credibility theory by evaluating the interplay of influencer credibility, trust, and attachment in shaping gamers’ microtransaction intentions.
k: influencer credibility; source credibility theory; influencer marketing; in-game purchases; live streaming

t: Integrating multi-modal data for enhanced heart disease prediction: an HPC-based clinical decision support system
a: Introduction Heart disease remains one of the leading causes of mortality worldwide, necessitating accurate and early prediction systems. Traditional methods often fail to effectively integrate diverse clinical data sources, creating a need for advanced, scalable solutions.Objectives This study aims to develop a High-Performance Computing (HPC)-based Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) for improved heart disease prediction using multi-modal healthcare data.Methodology The proposed system utilizes the Symile MIMIC dataset, which includes Electronic Health Records (EHR), time-series ECG signals, and medical imaging data. Categorical variables are encoded using label encoding techniques. Feature extraction is performed using specialized models: AlexNet for medical images, Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) for ECG time-series data, and a Feedforward Neural Network (FNN) for EHR data. The extracted features are integrated through a weighted feature fusion approach to enhance predictive performance. The model is implemented in Python and evaluated using standard performance metrics.Results Experimental findings demonstrate high predictive performance, achieving accuracy values of 0.987 and 0.988 for 70/30 and 80/20 training-testing splits, respectively, along with strong sensitivity, specificity, and precision.Practical Implications The proposed system offers a reliable and scalable solution for clinical decision-making, enabling early detection and improved management of heart disease in real-world healthcare settings.
k: heart disease prediction; clinical decision support systems; multimodal data integration; electronic health records; ECG time series; diagnostic imaging; feature fusion; high-performance computing; MIMIC dataset; early detection of heart disease

t: Werken voor essentie: Themanummer ‘Existentialisme in de arbeids- en organisatiepsychologie’
a: Samenvatting: Het existentialisme richt zich op de menselijke zijnsvraag. Doordat de mens zich bewust is van de eigen sterfelijkheid, moet deze zich daartoe in diens leven verhouden. Het zoeken naar betekenis binnen een wereld waarin deze niet vaststaat, is daarmee een ingewikkelde opgave. Existentialisme heeft grote raakvlakken met de psychologie, maar blijft zeldzaam binnen de arbeids- en organisatiepsychologie. Dit themanummer bevat drie bijdragen die elk op een andere manier het existentialisme toepassen op werk en organisaties. De eerste bijdrage betreft een existentialistisch perspectief op burn-out. Het artikel presenteert een meetinstrument voor existentiële bezorgdheden, gegrond in het werk, en verkent hoe deze samenhangen met burn-out. De tweede bijdrage positioneert leiderschap vanuit drie existentialistische denkers als een werkelijkheidsvormend handelen. Gezien hun prominente rol in organisaties heeft het gedrag van leiders een relevante impact op de realiteit van medewerkers. De derde bijdrage behandelt het concept nataliteit van Hannah Arendt in relatie tot werk, tegen de achtergrond van existentialisme. Waar het existentialisme uitgaat van de eindigheid van het leven, benadert Arendt betekenisvorming vanuit het vermogen om iets nieuws te beginnen. Met het existentialisme als vertrekpunt leveren de drie bijdragen nieuwe vragen en mogelijkheden op voor een ander en verderstrekkend begrip van werk- en organisatieleven.
k: existentialism; work psychology; organizational psychology; burnout; leadership; Hannah Arendt; pronatalism; meaning-making; finitude of life; death awareness

t: From Althusser to Foucault and Back: State, Discipline and Governmentality in the Crisis of Neoliberalism
a: Seeking a theoretical understanding of the current configuration of neoliberalism, the present article explores the following question: To what extent does Michel Foucault’s genealogy of governmentality advance or represent a retreat in relation to the framework found in Louis Althusser’s work? The investigation is guided by the hypothesis that the Foucauldian genealogy of discipline and governmentality can be understood as a concrete development of the idea of the political production of subjects defined in Althusser’s foundational text ‘Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses’. To do so, we map out how Althusser influenced Foucault, subsequently reflecting on the degree to which these Foucauldian formulations may contribute to a (re)reading of Althusser and so to a critique of both philosophers in favour of a framework of analysis better suited to the current state of capitalism.
k: Louis Althusser; Michel Foucault; governmentality; discipline; ideology; ideological state apparatuses; neoliberalism; crisis of neoliberalism; state; genealogy

t: Team Potency as a Driver of Higher and More Equal Task Contributions
a: Teams thrive when individuals converge around a shared goal. However, task contributions are not always evenly distributed among team members. Using the multilevel group process framework and consensus emergence modeling, we found that contribution patterns varied over time and across teams, suggesting team-specific rather than normative trajectories. Team potency beliefs positively predicted the initial team-level mean of task contributions, and this pattern was stable across time. Further, team potency beliefs positively predicted increasing similarity in contributions within teams across time. These findings highlight team potency as an internal driver of both higher-quality and more equal contributions within teams.
k: team potency; shared goals; group process; team dynamics

journal: Communications in Statistics: Theory and Methods
t: Sample size calculation in the presence of interval censor data using parametric illness-death variance inflation for mixed censoring (PIDV-MC) method
a: In clinical trials, particularly those evaluating progression-free survival (PFS) in oncology, mixed censoring arises where progression events are interval-censored due to periodic assessments, while death events are exactly observed. Traditional sample size methods, such as Schoenfeld’s formula, rely on the assumption of proportional hazards and the availability of exact event times (participant only to right-censoring). Consequently, these methods do not account for the information loss inherent in interval censoring, which effectively increases the variance of the estimator. This often results in underestimated sample sizes and underpowered studies. This paper introduces the Parametric Illness-Death Variance Inflation for Mixed Censoring (PIDV-MC) method, which models PFS within an illness-death framework and derives a variance inflation factor (VIF) using Fisher information to adjust for efficiency losses from interval censoring. Detailed derivations of the likelihood, Fisher information matrix, and adjustments are provided. Simulation studies across various scenarios demonstrate PIDV-MC’s superiority in achieving target power (80%) by increasing sample sizes in high-censoring conditions, compared to traditional approaches. The method enhances trial design reliability, especially when exact event times are unknown, emphasizing the importance of accounting for censoring uncertainty even with a fixed number of events.
k: sample size determination; interval censoring; illness-death model; variance inflation factor; Fisher information; progression-free survival; cancer clinical trials; power analysis

t: How Border Disputes Influence Disaster Response
a: This study examines how governments, international actors (states and international organizations), and non-state actors (non-governmental organizations) respond to disasters, focusing on whether response is distinct in border areas, in areas with ongoing territorial claims, and in areas with settled borders. The theory considers the role of state capacity and strategic importance of geographic areas to help understand whether and how government and other actors respond to disasters. Using new quantitative data on disaster response policies in Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru (1900–2020) at the administrative 1 level (N = 3,609), panel logit analyses show that territorial disputes significantly increase disaster response by security and international actors, and that disasters near international borders increase actors’ responsiveness, consistent with the strategic logic. In contrast, once a territorial claim is resolved, many actors (military, civil defense, leaders, IOs, and other states) are significantly less likely to offer disaster aid, reflecting the diminished strategic importance of the area. State capacity has a weaker effect on disaster response, although civil defense responds more often in more populated areas, and areas farther from the capital city receive less assistance from the military, civil defense, leaders, other states, and IOs. The findings demonstrate that geography and interstate relations influence disaster responses and that peaceful settlement of territorial disputes may paradoxically reduce disaster assistance.
k: disaster response; border disputes; territorial disputes; international boundaries; state capacity; strategic value; international organizations; non-governmental organizations; military assistance; civil protection; interstate relations; peaceful settlement of disputes; Latin America

t: Nudging provider adoption of clinical decision support: study protocol for a stepped-wedge cluster randomized, hybrid type III trial of an electronic health record-agnostic pulmonary embolism risk tool
a: BACKGROUND: About one-third of the computed tomography (CT) scans ordered yearly to evaluate for pulmonary embolism (PE) in emergency departments (ED) in the U.S. are avoidable. Clinical guidelines recommend the use of validated PE prediction rules which reduce CT scan ordering without an increase in missed PEs, but there is low provider adoption. Clinical decision support (CDS) that incorporates these rules along with nudges (subtle, non-coercive influences on decision-making) may improve provider adoption. In our pilot trial of a PE risk CDS tool with a nudge at order entry, adoption was significantly higher (39.1%) than for the tool without nudges (20.7%). The tool was developed on an EHR-agnostic web-based platform, designed for dissemination to work with any EHR. The objective of this study is to evaluate the tool with a nudge in a multi-site, randomized trial. METHODS: A hybrid type III, stepped-wedge, ED-level, cluster randomized trial will be conducted. Study settings include 12 EDs in three geographically diverse health care systems. The EDs will be randomized over 9 steps over 30 months, ensuring at least 3 months of intervention exposure for all EDs. We will randomize matched pairs of EDs based on patient volume in each stratum to early intervention or late intervention. All providers ordering CTs for the evaluation of PE in adult patients at the site EDs will be included. Our study will be guided by two complementary frameworks: Behavioral Change Wheel Framework and Proctor's Implementation Outcomes Framework. Nudge implementation strategies in the CDS user interface will be a peer comparison of providers' hit rates for CTs ordered for PE and salient messaging. We will use an EHR-agnostic, web-based platform to implement the tool. The primary outcome will be guideline-concordant CT ordering for PE. DISCUSSION: This trial will advance our understanding of the impact of behavioral strategies on improving provider adoption of CDS. Additionally, the trial will confirm the impact of guideline-concordant CT ordering on CT yield rates across a diverse patient population. The use of an EHR-agnostic platform helps maximize the dissemination potential of the core evidence-based practices it facilitates. TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT07249385; Registered 11/18/2025.
k: clinical decision support; nudging; pulmonary embolism; provider adoption; emergency department; guideline-concordant care; behavioral change strategies; implementation outcomes

t: The Core Concepts Express: Belgian Railways as a Teaching Case Connecting Policymaking, Governance, and Strategic Planning
a: Public affairs programs teach policymaking, governance, and strategic planning as core concepts, yet they are often taught in silos across separate courses. This separation, mostly reinforced by the legacy of the politics-administration dichotomy, leaves many learners able to define terms but less able to see how they co-exist and jointly shape strategic choices in public organizations. This integration gap is addressed here through a teaching case of NMBS/SNCB, Belgium’s state-owned rail operator. Set at headquarters in Brussels, it follows a strategy team preparing a planning-cycle briefing and provides traceable information on governance arrangements, policymaking, organisational positioning and capacities, and political context in a multi-actor governance setting. Exhibits support mapping steering signals and stakeholder pressures, identifying available discretion, and translating context into mandate-sensitive mission/vision language, prioritised strategic issues, and scenario-relevant uncertainties. The case builds analytical skills for connecting governance structures, policymaking dynamics, and strategic planning under contested expectations.
k: public affairs education; policy making; governance; strategic planning; politics-administration dichotomy; Belgian railways; state-owned enterprises; multi-actor governance; stakeholder pressure; scenario planning; mission and vision; public sector organizations

t: Transitioning to high-quality development: impact of AI pilot zones on digital technology innovation in China
a: Purpose This study aims to examine whether the New Generation AI Innovation and Development Pilot Zones policy, launched by China in 2019, promotes corporate digital technology innovation and identifies the boundaries of its impact. Design/methodology/approach This study integrates regional innovation system theory, information asymmetry theory, and dynamic capability theory. Using data from Chinese A-share companies from 2010 to 2024, we employ a staggered difference-in-differences model to examine the policy effects. Furthermore, through panel regression and heteroskedasticity tests, we observe how the policy effect varies across different firm characteristics. Finally, we examine the boundaries of the policy effect across firms with different financing constraints and dynamic capabilities. Findings First, the policy enhances corporate digital technology innovation. Second, the policy exhibits a certain degree of inclusiveness, with its impacts benefiting small- and medium-sized enterprises, non-high-tech companies, and firms in central and western regions, and it generates spillover effects. Third, the policy effect is weakened by firms' financing constraints. For firms under high financing constraints, engagement in AI strategic management can effectively mitigate the negative impact of financing constraints, and AI capital stock can also alleviate this negative impact to a certain extent. Finally, the policy-driven innovation improves corporate future sales and carbon productivity.
